THE FIRST PART — THE BOOKS

BOOK I — The Book of Chukwu

(Creation, Light, Cosmology)

Chapter 1 — Mbido Uwa

1 In the first age, before footsteps marked the earth and before names were firmly held, there was Chukwu, the Chi n’eke. He was unmade and unending, fullness without limit, light without fire, thought without tongue. Nothing stood outside Him, and nothing could contain Him. All that would ever be lived already rested within His being. 2 At that time, existence lay in deep stillness. Waters had not yet learned their paths, land had not yet hardened its skin, and spirits waited without dwelling. Silence covered all things, not as emptiness, but as sacred potential. 3 From within this Silence, Chukwu called forth Ana, the Sacred Earth. She did not arrive by force but by covenant. Ana became the Great Womb, the bearer of consequence and continuity. Upon Her body rose hills like bones, plains like open hands, and forests breathed from Her chest. Her veins became rivers, and Her memory became law. From that moment, no act upon Ana would be without meaning. 4 When Ana settled, Chukwu appointed the powers that would keep balance between sky, earth, and humanity. 5 He set Anyanwu in the sky, the Sun-Witness, opener of the day and revealer of truth. Anyanwu sees all deeds done upon Ana; nothing hidden survives his gaze. 6 He placed Onwa, the Moon, to govern time, rhythm, and return. Onwa taught the counting of days, the movement of blood, the seasons of planting and restraint. 7 He released Idemili, sacred water and python-spirit, into rivers and depths. Idemili carried purity and danger together. 8 He appointed Amadioha, thunder and lightning, as the voice of cosmic justice. When oaths were broken and abominations multiplied, Amadioha spoke from the sky, reminding the world that law precedes power. 9 Into the forests and crossroads, Chukwu sent Agwu, spirit of knowledge, madness, and revelation. Agwu opened the inner eye, calling diviners, healers, and vision-bearers. 10 He set Njoku deep within Ana’s soil, guardian of sustenance. Through Njoku, life learned patience, knowing that survival flows from harmony with land and season, not greed. 11 He raised Ikenga, the spirit of personal force and achievement, to stand with those who act with right intent. 12 At the boundaries, Ekwensu was stationed, the tester of intention, ensuring that no action is taken without moral weight.

Chapter 2 — Ụga Anọ — the Four Ages of the World

1 The world does not stand still, and it does not go forward only. It goes in ụga — and ụga is a cosmic age, an era, an epoch, a great turning of time, as oge is the ordinary word for time.

2 And there are four of them, and they come in order, and they come again.

3 Ụga Aka — the First Age. The age of the first being. There was no duality — a person and the world were not two things. There was profound wisdom, pure spirit and pure consciousness, men knew the whole of their own powers and the whole of the universal law, and there was no death.

4 Ụga Chi — the Second Age. The age of spirit. And duality came — the spiritual and the material separated, and a person became a self standing over against the world. There was a great influx of self-realised spirits, and soul-power, and ingenious cultural creation, and telepathy. And death appeared — for immortality was the privilege of the age before, and it was lost in this one.

5 Ụga Anwu — the Third Age. The age of light. And it is the age of the mind. Cosmic-minded visionaries — the Umu Anwu — are incarnated into it, and they are known by a deep solar intuition, a versatility of mind, and original thinking. It is the age of prophecy, of technological feats, and of a highly advanced understanding of energy and of how it plays upon consciousness throughout nature.

6 And in Ụga Anwu the urge to check harmful tendencies becomes a worldwide obsession. People become conscious of the land all at once, and are drawn to the ways of living and the thinking that keep it.

7 Ụga Azi — the Fourth Age. The age of degradation, also called Aka Aghali. And it is the age of wickedness. Pessimism, mindlessness, crass ignorance, wanton destruction, the desecration of natural harmony, a very low consciousness, superficiality, the disregard of sacred knowledge, greed beyond imagining, and conquest. In Ụga Azi the world is literally upside down — the descent of spiritual awareness.

8 And its mark is Ofeke — the consciousness of ignorance and vanity that fills the age. The ignorance of Ofeke clouds the mind, so that a person cannot reach his own higher self or look for a deeper truth. And a society in Ụga Azi is spiritually blind, taken up with appearance, and driven by short desires that end in long destruction.

9 And the world turns, and it turns back.

10 The four ages come in order as the sun crosses the sky — from Ụga Aka to Ụga Chi to Ụga Anwu to Ụga Azi. That is the clockwise turning, and it is the way down.

11 And at the end of Ụga Azi, the turning reverses, and time goes back the way it came — a person retraces his steps and corrects the road he took. The anti-clockwise turning is the way home.

12 And it does not leap. Humanity does not jump from Ụga Azi back to Ụga Aka. It goes back through them — and the going back is the point of the whole thing. Souls of Ụga Anwu rise again to bring liberation and healing; and from Ụga Anwu the world wakes into Ụga Chi, the age of spirit and of unity; and if it succeeds, it comes home to Ụga Aka, where all beings are one.

13 The anti-clockwise turn is the past, and the clockwise turn is the future, and where the two meet is the present. So the religion says that the present is not a point between two dead things. It is the place where the way down and the way home are both in a person's hand.

14 And a great cycle is called Mgba Ụga — eight ages in all, four going down and four coming back — and when the eight are complete the whole of created life takes one leap forward together, and that leap is Opupu Mmụọ, the coming-out of the spirit.

15 And a cycle that has been completed and receded is Ụga-Nala-Ana — one full completed cosmic cycle — and its knowledge and its wisdom are not lost, but are from that time reached for only through the open door of cosmic intuition.

16 And the next cycle is Opupu-Ije-Mmụọ, or Ụga Uwa, and it begins from an ascending point or a descending one — and with a matching influx of spirits being born into it.

17 Uje Ụga is an ascending cycle, and Una Ụga is a descending one.

18 And the religion says where we are. We are in an ascending turning, and the age before us is Ụga Anwu — the age of the mind, and of the visionaries of light. That is why this religion builds schools and not only shrines, and why it will not tell a person to put his mind away in order to be holy.

19 And the four seasons of the world are Ụga-Uwa-n'Anọ, and they have come and gone for as long as there has been creation — as the four days of the week have come and gone, Eke, Oye, Afo, Nkwo. The week is the age in small, and the age is the week writ large; that is the whole of the correspondence.

20 And so the religion is not permitted despair. This is the teaching of the ages, and it is the whole of what the religion draws from them: the descent is real, and the ascent is real, and they are the same road walked in two directions — and the religion exists to walk it back.

21 And the proverb of it is this: "Egbe belu, ugo belu, nke sị ibe ya ebena, nku kwaa ya." — Let the eagle perch, and let the kite perch; and if one denies the other, let its wings break. Light and dark, forward and backward, creation and destruction — each is there to hold the order, and each is an opportunity for renewal.

22 And so the religion does not say that this age is the last one. It says that this is the age in which the turning begins, and that the work of a person in it is the work of turning.

Chapter 3 — Uga Okike

1 When the earth was ready, Chukwu did not mould a figure from dust. Instead, He chose to grow the vessel of humanity like a sacred tree, allowing time and Ana to shape it. 2 Chukwu cast a Mkpuru-Ndụ (Seed of Life) into the ancient waters of Idemmili. It was small, but it held the heavy destiny of the Chi. Over cycles beyond counting, the seed sprouted, changing form as it crawled from the waters to the mud, and from the mud to the great forests. 3 Ndi-Enwe-Ohia (The Forest Dwellers): First, life grew into the high branches. These were the Ndi-Enwe-Ohia (The Forest Dwellers / Early Primates). They moved on four limbs, their eyes growing sharp to judge the distance between boughs. They lived in the safety of the leaves, eating the fruit that grew without labour. But Chukwu saw that their hands were occupied only with holding on, not with shaping the world. 4 Ndi-Kwụ-Ọtọ (The Standing Ones): Then, the world shifted. The forests shrank, and the grasslands of Ana opened wide. To survive, the creatures had to descend. Slowly, generation upon generation, they lifted their knuckles from the dirt. They became Ndi-Kwụ-Ọtọ (The Standing Ones / Australopithecus). By standing tall, they freed their hands from the burden of walking. They exposed their hearts to the wind and lifted their heads to see Anyanwu face-to-face. 5 Ndi-Nkà (The Skilled Artisans): As aeons passed, the spirit of Ikenga whispered to them. They realised their free hands could do more than hold; they could carve. They became Ndi-Nkà (The Skilled Artisans / Homo habilis). They picked up the stones of Ana and chipped them into blades. They broke the bone to find the marrow. With better food, their minds, the seat of Agwu, began to swell and spark. 6 Ndi-Njem (The Travelers): Then came the Ndi-Njem (The Travellers / Homo erectus). They were tall and strong, and they tamed the terror of the night: Fire (Ọkụ). With fire, they cooked, shrinking their jaws and growing their brains further. They walked out of the cradle of the sun, spreading across the earth, enduring cold and heat, testing the limits of the body. 7 Ndi-Dike-Ọgba (The Strong Ones of the Cave): Chukwu allowed the life-force to branch out, to see which wood was strongest for the carving. There were the Ndi-Dike-Ọgba (The Strong Ones of the Cave / Neanderthals). They were stocky and powerful as bears, surviving the bitter ice. They buried their dead and wore the skins of beasts, but the fullness of Chukwu’s intention did not settle upon them, and they eventually returned to the soil of Ana. 8 Ka Mma Dụ (Let Beauty Be & Let Goodness Be): Finally, on the dust of the original plains, the form was perfected. The throat changed, lowering to allow the voice to sing and name the spirits. The brain became a vast web of memory and foresight. 9 Chukwu looked upon this final vessel (Homo sapiens) and saw it was ready. He did not need to carve it anymore; the trials of the earth had carved it for Him. 10 Chukwu breathed Chi (the divine individual force) into them. He named them Mmadụ (Ka Mma Dụ), meaning “Let Beauty Exist” and “Let Goodness Be.” No longer just creatures of instinct, they became beings of Conscience. They could look at the Moon and measure time; they could look at the river and see Idemmili; they could look at each other and see the divine. 11 Thus, humanity was not made in a moment, but grown and carved in the fires of survival, rising from the water, down from the trees, and up from the dust, until they stood ready to hold the covenant with Chukwu.

Chapter 4 — The Nature of Chukwu

(Ife, Okike, Akala) 1 Chukwu is not a being among beings, but the ground of all being. He is not shaped by form, nor limited by place. Before matter gathered and before time learned to flow, Chukwu was, not as silence alone, but as meaning waiting to unfold. 2 Chukwu is Light: not light as flame or glare, but light as order, intelligibility, and truth. From this light came the laws by which stars burn, atoms bind, and life organises itself. Anyanwu is only a witness of this deeper light, for Chukwu’s radiance is the reason things can be known, distinguished, and understood at all. Where this light is present, confusion gives way to pattern; where it is resisted, disorder follows. 3 Chukwu is Creator/Inventor, yet He does not create by haste or whim. His creation is lawful becoming. He brings forth worlds by setting principles into motion, gravity, rhythm, variation, balance. Through Ana, the Earth, creation takes form slowly: stone remembers pressure, water remembers flow, life remembers adaptation. Chukwu does not interrupt nature; nature is His method. Every species, every transition, every extinction is part of a wider creative unfolding. 4 Chukwu is Destiny: not fate that crushes choice, but direction that gives meaning. Destiny in Chukwu is the tendency of existence toward complexity, awareness, and responsibility. From simple matter to living cells, from living cells to thinking beings, destiny moves not in a straight line but in patient curves. Humanity stands within this destiny, not as its end, but as its conscious participant. Choice does not oppose destiny; it fulfils it.

Chapter 5 — Iji Ana — the Harmonising of the Ground

1 The ground is not only to be kept clean. It is to be brought into order — and the science of that is Iji Ana, also spoken Iji Ana and Iji Ani: geodesy, one of the sacred sciences the Igbo demonstrated a mastery of.

2 And what it does is bring the harmony of the sky down to the earth — Anakwudo-ma-Enukwudo, that which is above is joined to that which is below — and it is not one thing but many, a meta-science, driven by exact thinking rather than by sentiment.

3 And the oldest work of it in this land was the raising of the mound — Ikwunite-Aba-Igwe, the raising of the crown of the celestial mound — and the settlements were built on it.

4 And the house itself is ensouled. A house is not lived in until it is brought into order, and the religion keeps that: the ground is asked, the surfaces are marked with nzu, the water is poured, and the white cloth is laid — and the house is entered.

5 And the house is un-ensouled when its people are gone. A house whose dead have not been released is not a house — and this is why the burial is a matter of the ground and not only of the body.

6 And the same is done for the environs. The compound, the path, the market, the approach to the Ndose — each is brought into order in its own measure, and the religion holds that a place kept in order holds its people in order.

7 And the specialists of it were the ritual-kings, and their names are in the land still: Eze Akum, Eze Okpoko, Eze Ana, Eze Mkpume, Eze Uzu, Eze Oba — and they were technocrats, and among their offices was the mastery of the elements.

8 And the lineages are still there. Umu Mkpume of Oba in Anambra, whose tradition says their ancestors were unequalled at working stone and mineral, and Uzu Akoli, whose stones are the finest in the land. And the proverb of it is this: "Okwute hiri ehi, too ato na Uzu Akoli, o zi mbunata." — durable stones lie in their formations at Uzu Akoli; it is only a matter of carrying them to the site.

9 And the religion draws the doctrine out of all of it. A shrine, a grove, a temple, a church, a mosque, an oracle-place — these are not divine things. They are sanctified places. The human being is divine, and nature is divine, and no building is.

10 And the doctrine of a doctrine is not divine either. What is divine is a person's own experience of the truth in it — and that is why this religion says again and again that a symbol is not a device and a mark does not act. nzu at the door does not keep anything out; it says that the door is kept.

11 So a person comes to the sacred place for three things, and the religion names them:

12 Isa Ajasinobi — to revive the devotion that has gone stale in him; 13 Ichikota-Uche-na-Mmụọ — to gather his mind and his spirit back and set them again; 14 and Inye-Ikenga-Nni — to feed the ikenga — to put strength back into the force of his own right hand.

15 And none of that is done to him by the place. The place is where he does it, and the priest is not a man who has the thing and gives it out: he is a man who was called and readied from birth for the work, and his office is to keep the order — Udo, the harmony — standing on his chi, on his ogu, and on the ofo of his ancestors.

16 And the work is Iji Ana, and it is never finished, for the ground is brought into order, and then it is kept.

Chapter 6 — Iwu Ana

(Convenant of Ana) 1 When Mmadụ stood fully upright, possessing the fire of intelligence and the spark of the Chi, Chukwu saw that this power was dangerous. A beast kills from hunger, but a human can kill from greed, envy, or pride. To prevent Mmadụ from destroying the very earth that birthed him, Chukwu bound humanity to Ana through Nso Ana, the Sacred Taboos. 2 This was not merely a rulebook, but a survival strategy. It was the wisdom of aeons condensed into law, ensuring the community (Obodo) could thrive where the solitary animal would perish. 3 The Sanctity of Blood (Ndụ): Thou shalt not shed the blood of a kinsman upon the soil. 4 In the wild, the strong eat the weak. But Mmadụ was forged to survive through unity. Chukwu taught that the life-force (Ndụ) is a stream that flows through all kin. To cut a kinsman is to cut one’s own root. If blood is spilt in anger, the Earth is defiled, and Idemmili withdraws her waters until the land is cleansed. 5 This ensured that the newly evolved humans solved conflict through council (Ndi Ako), not slaughter. 6 The Integrity of Speech (Eziokwu): Thou shalt not break an oath made on the Ofo. 7 Animals have voices, but only Mmadụ has the Word. Speech is the tool of order. If words lose their meaning, society collapses back into the silence of the forest. Amadioha watches the tongue; he strikes those who swear falsely to deceive their brothers. 8 This fostered trust, the foundation of trade and complex society. 9 The Purity of Lineage (Mmụbụ): Thou shalt not know the body of thy closest kin. 10 The Forest Dwellers mated without distinction, but Mmadụ was given the foresight of generations. Chukwu revealed that strength lies in diversity. To turn inward is to breed weakness and rot. Ana, the Earth force, forbids incest (Alu), pushing humanity to seek partners outside their immediate circle. 11 This ensured genetic diversity and health, preventing the species from withering. 12 The Respect of Boundaries (Oke): Thou shalt not shift the landmark of a neighbour. 13 As Njoku taught the cultivation of yam, land became life. Greed for land brings war. Ekwensu tempts the hand to steal, but the Covenant declares that a boundary stone, once set by the elders, is sacred. To move it is an act of war against peace itself. 14 This established the concept of property and respect for the rights of others, vital for agricultural settlement. 15 The Protection of the Vulnerable (Nnete): Thou shalt not mistreat the stranger, the child, or the elder. 16 A society is judged by how it treats its weakest link. Elders hold the memory of the species; children hold the future. Even the stranger is a test of character. Chukwu decreed that hospitality is a sacred duty, for every stranger could be a spirit in disguise. 17 This built the strong communal safety nets that define Igbo society. 18 The Staff of Authority (Ofo na Ogu): To seal this Covenant, Chukwu gave Mmadụ the Ofo, a branch from the sacred Detarium tree. The Ofo is the physical staff of truth. It does not decay easily, just as truth must not decay. 19 He paired it with Ogu, the principle of innocence. Before any man can act or judge, he must look at his hands and say, “Ejim Ofo na Ogu” (I hold the staff of truth and the peace of innocence). Only he whose hands are clean can call upon the spirits for aid. 20 Thus, Mmadụ walked the earth not as a conqueror, but as a gardener and a guardian, holding the balance between the Sky (Enu) and the Earth (Ana), bound by the laws that keep chaos at bay.

Chapter 7 — The Four Strangers

A story of the beginning of the markets.

1 In the beginning of the markets, Chukwu sent strangers to the Ikala.

2 Four of them came, and each carried a basket. They came to the head town and stood before the head, and they refused to disclose their names.

3 The head received them, and gave them food, and said nothing. But in the night he sent rats into their baskets — and the rats turned the things in the baskets, and the things named the men in the morning light.

4 And when the sun came up, the head called them by name:

5 Eke! Oye! Ofo! Nkwo! — and he called them by the names he had found. The second day is Oye in the old speech of Ide, and Orie in the speech of the centre — and the story keeps Oye in this telling, and either name in the mouth of a person praying.

6 And the people praised the wisdom of the head.

7 And the four days are one week, and the week is called Izu. And every market of the land is held on one of the four, so that a person who walks out on Eke knows whose ground he is standing on. And the four strangers spoke, and said:

"Have four markets and four days. Call them Eke, Oye, Afo, Nkwo."

8 And they vanished.

Chapter 8 — The Famine, and the Yam

A story of the beginning of the markets.

1 In the first years of the markets, the rain failed. It failed in the planting season, and it failed in the season after, and men looked at the sky until their necks ached.

2 The yam rotted in the barn before it was put in the ground, and what was put in the ground did not come up. The cocoyam withered at the root. The maize stood thin and yellow and gave nothing, and the vegetable that women had kept by the water dried where it grew.

3 And the people ate what they had never eaten. They ate the bark of the ogilisi and the root of the wild yam that bites the tongue. They ate the seed kept for the next planting, and then they had no seed. And they ate the earth of the termite hill, which fills a belly and gives nothing back.

4 The old died first, and then the children. And the mothers went about with dry breasts and did not speak.

5 And in the third year, Ikala the head of the religion went up to the shrine, and he called on Chukwu.

6 He did not go with the town behind him. He went alone, and he broke the kola himself, and poured the wine on the ground, and named his own chi and the chi of every person he could think of.

7 And he said:

"You gave us the ground, and the ground has stopped.

You gave us the rain, and the rain has gone elsewhere.

We have done what we were taught. Show us what we were not taught."

8 And he waited seven days. And on the seventh day he heard it, and the word was not what he had asked for.

9 And Chukwu said:

"Offer your first son, and your first daughter."

10 And the head of the religion came down from the shrine and did not eat, and he did not tell the town that day or the next. He called the elders, and the Ndi Nze, and the Nzemabua, and the diviners, and he set the word before them.

11 And they were silent a long while. And then the diviners threw, and threw again, and the afa did not contradict the word. And the Nzemabua said that the word was clear, and the head said that it was clear, and that being clear did not make it easy.

12 And then they sent for the man, and he came.

13 He was a farmer of the lowest quarter of the town, and his name was Ezeji — the king of yam — and he had never had a yam worth the name. He had two children and a wife, and one plot, and nothing else.

14 And they told him the word.

15 And he did not refuse. He asked one question: whether the ground would bear after it. And they told him that they did not know, and that the word said only that the offering be made.

16 And he said: "Then let it be made, and let the town eat."

17 And his wife did not speak for three days, and on the fourth she washed her children and oiled their heads and put their best cloth on them, and she did not ask them to be brave, and she did not tell them why.

18 The son was called Ezeji after his father, and he was eleven years old and he could take a goat to market on his own. The daughter was called Oliaku, and she was nine, and she could carry water from the stream on her head without spilling it.

19 And they were given the Ichi marks. The elder drew the lines on their faces while they sat still — for the mark of the covenant was cut on a person who was old enough to sit still and young enough to be told to. And the town was called, and the town stood and watched the marks being cut, because nothing that was done to a child was done in a corner.

20 And for twelve days they were kept. They were fed well, and they were not made to work, and they were taken to see the market and the river and the standing stones, and on each of the twelve days the elder who kept them told them what the town was and how it had come to be.

21 And the elder did not tell them that they were going to die. He told them what a town is for. And when he had finished, he told them what would be asked, and he told them plainly.

22 And the son said: "Then let the town live." And the daughter said: "Will the water be there, where we are going?" And the elder said that it would. And she was glad, because she carried water.

23 And on the twelfth night they were laid on the ground of the shrine, and the town stood around them, and the head of the religion did the office.

24 And the offering was made.

25 And the town went home, and the market was not held on the next day, and not on the day after it.

26 And on the third morning a woman went up to the shrine to sweep, because sweeping is the first act of the religion and the shrine was hers to sweep.

27 And the ground where the son had been laid had opened, and out of it had come the yam — the long yam, heavy and white, and beside it the palm, standing as a tree where no tree had stood.

28 And on the ground where the daughter had been laid there was cocoyam, and maize with its hair out, and the vegetable that grows by water.

29 And she stood in the middle of them and shouted.

30 And the town came up the hill, and stood, and looked, and did not go near the soil.

31 And the head of the religion came, and he looked long, and he called the elders and the Nzemabua, and the diviners threw over the new ground and the afa answered.

32 And Chukwu said:

"Distribute all these to all the Igbo, and receive tribute from them."

33 And the head of the religion took the first yam in his two hands and held it up so that the whole town saw it, and he said the words, and the town answered.

34 And they did not eat it that day. The first of it was cut and laid on the shrine, and the Ndi Nze carried what remained to the four quarters, and every household got a piece, and the family of Ezeji got the portion of the two.

35 And the tribute was set. Every household that took the seed gave back the first of what it grew — to the shrine, and to the old, and to the household that had none. And that is the first-fruits, and it is kept to this day.

36 And the father of the two did not take double. He took his portion as the others took theirs, and he said that he had not bought the yam with a child; he had given the child, and the yam had been given, and the two were not a trade.

37 And he planted the whole of his portion and ate none of it, and the year after he had yam enough to give tribute twice, and he was called Ezeji for the rest of his life and it was no longer a joke.

38 And the daughter's name was given to the water — for the place where she had been laid was the place the new seed came from, and the women who carried water to the shrine called it Oliaku's place, and the market of the fourth day takes its name from it.

Chapter 9 — Eri, and His Son

A memorial of the head town.

1 Eri came to the valley of the river, and settled there — at the place the tradition names, on the Omambala.

2 And Eri had a son, and the son stayed in the place his father had chosen, and did not go out to take other men's land by war.

3 He took nothing by war. He took it by the shrine and by the word. He settled, and he kept the rites, and the settlements round about began to send to him — first for judgement, and then for the blessing of their own shrines, and then for the confirming of their chiefs.

4 And the name of the son became the name of a people, so that to this day a child of that line carries it — at the beginning of his name or at the end of it.t the end of it — and the tradition holds that the son is born again in his own grandchildren.

5 And the Ikala came to be called the one who is half human and half spirit — for he rules in the world of the living and is answerable in the world of the dead.

BOOK II — The Book of Ana

(Earth, Morality, Purity, Human Conduct)

Chapter 1 — The Soil as Witness

1 Ana does not sleep. She records every footprint, every spill of blood, every whispered curse. Just as the stars retain their light for centuries, Ana retains the memory of every deed done upon her breast. Therefore, let no man spit upon the earth in contempt, for he spits upon the face of his mother. Let no man poison her rivers with the waste of metal or greed, for Idemmili will withdraw her fertility, and the yam will rot in the barn.

2 And Ana is not merely the ground beneath a man's feet. She is the living earth, and the judge of what is done upon her — and the religion holds that the ground of a place keeps what has been done on it. and the religion calls the record she keeps Aka Ose. Every deed, and every word, and every thought leaves its trace in it, and nothing is lost. The ground of a town is not neutral, and it is not a floor. It remembers what it was made to carry.

Chapter 2 — Ana, the Way to Chukwu

1 Ana is the mother earth. She is the ground under the foot, and the field that feeds, and the body that receives the dead back. She is called Ana, and Ana, and Anị in the old speech, and the names are one name.

2 And Ana and Ana are the same, and this religion does not hold two earth mothers. They are two names of one mother, and a person who keeps them apart has made two things out of one thing.

3 And the word ana is also the ordinary word for ground, and land, and a plot, and the soil of a town — and she is called by it because she is it. The name did not come from the word; the word came from the thing. So Ana mmụọt, the spirit-land, is a place within her and is not another mother; and the ground of a compound is a part of her and is not a likeness of her; and the earth a person stands on at his door is herself, and not a reminder of her.

4 And the religion uses both names freely, and means one being by both, and sets no rank between them. A prayer that says Ana and a prayer that says Ana are the same prayer. And no one is to be corrected for using the one and not the other — for they are the same, and the correcting of a person over the name of his own mother is not a work of this religion.

5 And it is said here once, so that it is never in doubt: Ana is Ana, and Ana is Ana, and Anị in the old speech is the same again. One mother. Many names. No second.

6 And she is not one thing among the many things of the world. Everything that lives, lives upon her and out of her, and returns to her. There is no creature that does not begin in her and end in her, and there is no rite of this religion that does not touch her.

7 And Chukwu is the source, and the light, and the thought that has no tongue — and the religion says plainly that a person does not go to Chukwu directly. Not because Chukwu is angry, and not because a person is unworthy, but because that is how the making was done: the far is far, and the near is near.

8 And Ana is the near one. She is under the feet and not above the head. She is the one a person touches without knowing he touches her, and walks on without greeting her, and is fed by without thanking her.

9 And through Ana the heart of Chukwu is reached. This is the doctrine of this religion, and it is the whole of the doctrine of the way. She is the road. Not a road among roads, and not the nearest road, but the road. So a person who would be heard by Chukwu goes first to the ground he stands on, and is honest there, and only then looks up.

10 And this is why the religion says what it says to a person who wishes to become an Odianian. The one belief required is belief in Ana. Nothing else is asked at the door. A person may come from any town, any house, any tongue, and may know nothing else of this religion at all. But he must believe in the mother earth — and the belief is not a word spoken once; it is a way of walking, and of eating, and of taking, and of putting things down.

11 And what believing in her means, since the word alone is cheap.

12 That the ground is alive and is not a floor. A person who believes in Ana does not foul her, and does not poison her water, and does not take from her in greed, and does not move her boundaries in the night.

13 That she remembers. Every deed, and every word, and every thought leaves its trace, and nothing is lost — and this is Aka Ose, the record she keeps.

14 That her memory is the law. Whatever the law of this religion says, it says it because the ground holds it.

15 That she receives the dead. A person who believes in Ana does not fear to lie down in her at the end, for she is the one who took him in at the beginning.

16 And that a person is judged by her and not merely by men. The look of the thing and the truth of it are not the same, and it is Ana who holds the difference.

17 And the religion keeps one thing absolutely clear here, and will not let it be blurred. Ana is not Chukwu. She is not the source and she is not the maker of what has no end. She is the mother, and the way, and the mediator, and she is honoured as those are honoured — and a person who worships Ana as though she were Chukwu has made an idol of his own road and has lost the way he was standing on.

18 And the religion says why the road runs through her and not around her. Because Chukwu is far and she is near. Because Chukwu is light and she is ground. The light a person cannot stand in and hold; the ground he stands on all his life. And because she is the mother, and a mother is what a person goes through to reach the father of the house — not because the father is hidden, but because the mother is the one who carried him there.

19 And so the first altar of this religion is not in the temple. It is the ground the person is standing on. A temple is built so that a person may come to Ana together with others, and on clean ground, and in one place — but the ground came first, and the temple is her house and not her replacement.

20 And the ancestors enter through her also. The Ndi Eri are in her keeping, and it is from her that the living walk over them and the dead are sent back through her. So a person who honours the dead and despises the ground has honoured nobody, and has said a word over an empty seat.

21 And the religion's word on the whole of it: a person may believe in many things and reach nothing. But whoever believes in Ana and walks on her as on a mother will find that the way is already under him. And the heart of Chukwu is at the end of it.

Chapter 3 — Nso

1 Nso is the law of what is set apart. And it is two things in one word, and the person who keeps only one of them has kept nothing.

2 The first face of Nso is the boundary — the thing a person must not do, because doing it takes him away from what he is. And it is not kept because the thing is evil in itself. It is kept because the thing is not good for this person.

3 A thing that feeds one man will sicken another, and the second man is not therefore cursed. Some thrive in the crowd and are wasted in solitude; some think only in solitude and are scattered in the crowd. So a prohibition is not an accusation. It is a line drawn round something worth keeping.

4 The second face of Nso is the thing a person must preserve — and it is the greater half, and it is the half that is forgotten. Not "what must I avoid," but: what must I keep doing if I am to remain myself?

5 And the religion says a life is shaped by both. The boundary keeps a man from what weakens him; the devotion keeps what strengthens him. The river is powerful because it has banks. And the man who only avoids, and preserves nothing, becomes careful and empty.

6 And Nso is not a punishment, and it is not a trap. It does not grow angry when a person wanders. It goes on pointing, as a compass points in a bag, waiting to be taken out.

7 And the religion's floor. Some things are not personal at all, and no man's Nso may license them: truth-speaking, and compassion, and justice, and humility, and respect for other people. These are the ground every house stands on. Nso begins where they become particular to one life.

8 Two men may both hold to honesty, and for one it means he will not exaggerate his own doings, and for the other it means he will not carry tales at all, for he knows how easily a tale carries him. The value is common to both. The boundary belongs to each.

9 And so every person's Nso is his own, and it differs, as faces differ. Human beings were not made to flourish under one set of conditions. If our lives are different, why should one man's discipline be assumed to serve all men?

10 And the personal Nso of a person is his Iwu Chi — the law of his own chi — and it is written nowhere but in his life. So it is read, as a path is read, and not issued as a command is issued.

11 And how a person comes to know it. It is discovered, and it is seldom invented. It comes out of observation, and reflection, and experience, and failure, and growth, and the company a man keeps; and over years the pattern becomes impossible to ignore, so that his own life has been his teacher. The man who sits down and decides what his Nso shall be has written himself a set of rules and called it a law of the spirit.

12 And the mark of a true Nso is one sentence, and every person will know it when he hears it in himself: "Whenever I cross this line, I lose something that matters." The loss may be of the body, or of the spirit, or of the work. Whatever it is, it repeats.

13 And it is found on both hands — from what weakens and from what strengthens. A man notices that he does his best work after an hour alone: that hour may be a thing to preserve. He notices that after three hours of the town's noise his patience is gone: that may be a thing to keep out.

14 And the religion warns against one thing above all others here. Do not take another man's Nso and wear it. We admire a man's discipline and copy the whole of it, without knowing what it is holding up. Your Nso should make you more fully yourself, and not a likeness of him.

15 And a person's Nso does not come from one place. It comes from three things together, and none of the three is enough alone.

16 From what is inherited — the wisdom of the house and of the town, which exists because those before us watched what made a people flourish. And it is understood and applied, and not merely repeated. A man who keeps his father's Nso without understanding it is keeping a custom, and he has not kept a law.

17 From what the calling requires — for purpose reveals not only what a person should do but what he must protect. A writer must preserve time for thought; a leader his integrity; a healer his compassion; a teacher his curiosity. And the clearer the work becomes, the more particular the Nso becomes.

18 And from what the person chooses — for neither the house nor the calling takes away his own decision, and character is made of ordinary decisions repeated. And it is here that a man either keeps what he was given or lets it go with his hands open.

19 And the religion's word on the three: freedom without any boundary leads back into bondage, and the work of a life is to choose the right boundaries and keep them. A house is built of all three — what is inherited is the ground, what the calling requires is the plan, and what the person chooses is whether the house is built at all.

20 And Nso Ana is the Nso of the land, and it is not personal. It is one law for the whole town, and it is the religion's oldest law — and it is set out where the ground is set out.

21 And the Nso of the land, in short, is this: no ground is fouled and left so; no water is poisoned; no boundary is moved in the night; no sacred place is entered as a market is entered; and nothing that lives is killed for cruelty, or for display, or for sport. The land is a witness, and it is not a floor.

22 And the Nso of the kola is set under the Nso of the land, for the kola is the tree of hospitality and of prayer, and it is not to be mishandled. Oji is the sign of life, and of welcome, and of the word spoken between people.

23 And the rule is this: a person does not pluck the kola before it is ripe. Oji anaghị ami ami — the kola tree does not bear as other trees bear. Oji na abịa abịa — the kola arrives. It comes into being at its own pace. It is not produced.

24 And the offence of taking it early is not that the kola is spoiled. It is that the time was overruled. It is impatience, and it is disregard for the order of things, and it is the interruption of a process that had not finished itself.

25 And the signs of ripeness are read, and not guessed: some of the green leaves turn, shifting into yellow and into brown; the tree begins to shed some of its own leaves; and the pod loses the deep green of its growing and shows that it is done. These are the kola's own word that its cycle is complete.

26 And the religion takes the teaching out of the tree and puts it where people live. Not everything is taken in haste, and not everything that can be forced should be forced. Some things must mature and reveal themselves; and what is taken before its time is not only green — it is spoiled in the taking. And this is true of an opportunity, and of a relationship, and of knowledge, and of a person's own growth.

27 And the whole of the kola's law is patience. Respect for the process; trust in the timing; and attention to the cycles of things. And the one who waits for the kola to arrive is not slow. He is keeping the law of the land.

Nchọpụta Nso — the rite of discerning a person's own Nso

28 And because the personal Nso is discovered and not issued, the religion keeps a rite for the discovering, and it is Nchọpụta Nso. And it is kept with a Dibia, and over weeks, and not in an hour. A person should keep the questions himself for a year first, and he should. But the rite is kept with a reader, for a man is blind in his own case.

29 And these are the questions of Nchọpụta Nso, in the order the religion puts them.

30 The turning points. What moments changed me permanently? Which of my choices strengthened me further than I expected? Which of my mistakes did damage beyond the one part of my life they touched? And what lesson keeps returning until I learn it?

31 The two lists. What quietly strengthens me, and what quietly weakens me. And the mark of these is that nobody watching would see them happen, and their effect is still there long after.

32 What I take in. For one week the person notes what he has consumed — what he watched, what he read, what he listened to, whose talk he sat in, what he looked at. And then he asks of each thing: does this leave me clearer, or less clear? And: if what I take in is making my habits, what am I making?

33 The body's testimony. For one month the person notes how his body answers what he does to it — the food, the company, the room, the hours, the work. The body speaks first and is the last thing a man listens to. And where the body is sick, the religion sends the person to a healer of the body, and does not read the sickness as a verdict.

34 The gift and its conditions. What are my gifts, and when do they come? What hour, what company, what silence do they need? And what am I doing that keeps them away?

35 And the cost of the crossing. Think of the times I knew, and did it anyway. What did I ignore? Why did I ignore it? What happened after? Which part of my life suffered first? And how long did the coming back take? Sometimes a man's consequences reveal his Nso more clearly than his successes do.

36 And last, the writing of it. The person writes two lists with his own hand, and the Dibia keeps a copy: what I must preserve, and what I must avoid. And every line is marked Ihe Dị Mkpa (essential), Ihe Bara Uru (important), or Ihe Nhọrọ (optional). And no list is longer than the person can carry. A Nso of forty lines is not a law; it is an ambition.

37 And the last question of the rite is asked aloud, and is not written:

"Ọ bụrụ na m dịrị ndụ dịka iwu ndị a ruo afọ ise, onye ka m ga-abụ?"

If I live by these for five years, who will I become?

38 And if the answer is a person worth becoming, the rite is kept, and the list is read aloud once a year at Igu Aro, with the year's other reckonings. And it may be amended, for a man at forty is not the man he was at twenty-five. The principles hold; the expression matures. It is a garden and not a stone tablet. The gardener's commitment stays, and the work of the season changes.

39 And a household may keep a Nso of its own, and a Ndose may keep a Nso of its own. And these are written also, and read also, and amended also. So a house knows what it is for, and a town knows what it is for, and nobody has to guess.

The drift, and the return

40 And the breaking of Nso is rarely done in one act. It is done by inches. A man stops keeping one promise to himself. He becomes used to "just this once." He puts off the difficult words. He lets one practice go, and then another. And over time his standard moves, and what was once uncomfortable becomes ordinary. And this is the most dangerous state of all, because it never once feels dramatic. A ship that alters its course by one degree appears to be holding the same course, and weeks later it comes to a different country.

41 And these are the signs that a person has drifted from his own Nso.

42 He no longer feels like himself, and people praise his work while something in him is wrong. "I do not know what has come over me."

43 The practices that once held him up have quietly gone — and he never decided to abandon them; they went one at a time. And they are always the first things sacrificed when life presses hard.

44 He is busy, and he is not fulfilled. And the business has become a way of not noticing that he has drifted.

45 His body keeps interrupting him — exhaustion, broken sleep, tension, headaches, a mind that will not hold. And here the religion says plainly: these things have many causes, and a person must be examined by those who know the body, and a reading of afa is not a substitute for that. Spiritual interpretation must never become an excuse for neglecting a treatable sickness.

46 The small compromises have become easy, and he is ignoring what he already knows. "I know I do not sleep enough." "I know I should not speak when I am angry." "I know I need the quiet." The trouble is almost never that a man does not know. It is that he has not been faithful to what he already knew.

47 And his gifts have become hard to reach. The gift has not gone anywhere. The conditions in which it grows have gone.

48 And the religion's word on the return. A person who has drifted does not need a great rite. He needs to begin again, in small and ordinary things. Rest. One practice taken up again. One walk. One honest word. One promise to himself kept. Great restoration begins in small faithfulness.

49 And the road back is the second face of Nso, and it is not a new law. A man returns by preserving again what was set apart for him.

50 And where the drift has touched the ground, or an oath, or another person, the return is Ichu Aja, which is set out in the Book of Rites — and the first step of it is always the putting down of the thing itself. No list is amended to cover a debt that can simply be paid.

The Nso that is kept by every person alike

51 And of the Nso of the body, which is one law for everybody.

52 Nso Aka — the purity of the hands. A man washes before he touches the Ofo, and before he handles food for others. The profane must not handle the sacred.

53 Anuri — the purity of eating. Life is sacred within the order of Ana, and so the taking of life is done without needless cruelty. And what is eaten is wholesome: not carrion, not what died of itself, and not the flesh of an animal that suffered needlessly before its death. The stomach is the first temple of Chi, and it is not defiled with rot, nor with scavengers, nor with flesh taken in cruelty.

54 And the religion's word on the killing of animals: an animal is killed out of use, and never for display, and never in cruelty — and it is killed quickly, and its blood goes to the ground. And it is killed at the rites and the festivals of this religion, as it always has been.

55 Nso Arụ — the purity of the body. The body is the shrine of the Chi, and it is not to be mutilated to deny its form, nor masked in deceit. You are as you were made.

56 And the affections of the heart are a deep river, and Chukwu does not police the river's current. If a man's courage is made stronger by the arm of a man, or a woman's peace is found in the bosom of a woman, they may build a household together. And they take the oath upon the Ofo before the elders — for the bond is tested not by the sex of the beloved, but by the truth of their work, the protection they give the vulnerable, and the honour they bring to their lineages.

57 And they are counted among the households of the Ndose, and their children are called Ụmụ Oyo, the children of love. The religion condemns the shedding of blood, and the shifting of boundaries, and the breaking of oaths. It does not condemn loyal love that builds and protects.

58 And the religion does not count among the faithful the one who denies his own making — the man who says he is a woman, or the woman who says she is a man — for such a one does not worship Chukwu, but his own crafting. And this is a hard word, and the religion does not soften it: what was made is not to be denied.

Chapter 4 — Alu, the Abominations

1 Alu is an abomination — a wrong that the ground itself holds, and not the person only. So Nso may be a man's own business. Alu is the town's.

2 And the religion's first word on Alu is a caution. When misfortune comes upon a town — flood, or blight, or pest among the crops, or sickness among the animals, or deaths that come too many at once — the people shall seek the natural causes first, and shall not begin by assuming that Ana is angry. The elders, and the farmers, and the healers, and those who know the water and the land shall examine the ground, and the water, and the animals, and the practices of the people. And then what can be corrected shall be corrected, for a fault in the land, or in a practice, is answerable by work and not by an offering.

3 And Alu is these, and they are few, and they are grave.

4 The spilling of kin-blood. To kill a kinsman is to cut the root of the family tree. The killer owes Iwu to the family — the seven cows and a maiden, as the old law had it, or its worth in the reckoning of the council — and if he refuses, the matter passes to the law of the land. The religion does not call down lightning upon him. It puts the debt into the hands of the living.

5 The shifting of a boundary. A boundary stone set by the elders is a piece of Ana's skeleton. To move it in the night for more farmland is to steal from the whole town's soul. So the stone is put back, and the one who moved it makes his acknowledgement in the open, and what he took is returned with more. A white he-goat was killed for this in the old practice, and the religion keeps the he-goat — and it is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled on the ground, and not poured over the altar. And the stone is put back, and the ground returned.

6 Incest. Union with one's mother, or sister, or daughter, or any close relative is forbidden. It blinds the line of sight to the ancestors. And a union so made is Nkpagbu, a lost echo — it cannot inherit, and it cannot hold land.

7 The breaking of an oath sworn upon the Ofo. A man who swears falsely upon the Ofo kills his own spirit. He is put out of the square until he confesses in the open, and his word is not taken again in the town until the council says otherwise.

Chapter 5 — Ikocha Ana, the Cleansing of the Earth

1 Ikocha Ana is the cleansing of the ground, and it is kept by the whole town and not by one person.

2 When the town is struck — flood, or blight, or pest among the crops, or sickness among the animals, or deaths too many at once — the people shall first seek the natural causes, and shall not begin by assuming that Ana is angry.

3 So the elders, and the farmers, and the healers, and those who know the water and the land shall examine it: the ground, the water, the animals, the practices of the people, and what has been done to the place. And they shall say what they find, and not what is convenient.

4 And what can be corrected shall be corrected — the land restored, the water protected, the disease treated, the damage repaired, and the harmful practice changed. This part is not a rite. It is work, and it comes first.

5 And then, and only then, the Dibia keeps Ikocha Ana.

6 Clean water is poured upon the earth, and the people give thanks to Ana, and they say aloud what they have learned.

7 And a white stone is set in the ground — and it is Ncheta Nkwa, the memory of a promise — and it stands for the responsibility the town has taken for its own ground. It is not a payment. It is a reminder, and it is put where people walk past it.

8 And the meaning of the whole rite is this: to honour Ana is to understand the ground, and to protect what lives on it, and to correct the harm we have done. A town that pours its water and changes nothing has performed the rite and kept none of it.

9 And Ikocha Ana is kept with an animal where the harm done to the ground is grave — a fowl for a light wrong, and a he-goat where the ground was badly fouled — and the blood is spilled into the earth that was harmed. The ground is fed as well as swept, for the earth is a living thing and not a floor.

Chapter 6 — Afa and Moral Disorder

1 When afa is consulted concerning a moral disorder, its signs are read as signs of harmony or of imbalance — and never as automatic proof that a particular person is guilty. A reading that condemns a man by itself has been read wrongly.

2 And the signs may point to deceit, or injustice, or a broken obligation, or harmful conduct, or a quarrel not yet settled, or the need for cleansing. And the Dibia shall read the signs together with the facts of the matter — and where the facts are not known, the reading does not supply them.

3 And where wrongdoing is established, the remedy is not vengeance. It is the correction of the harm, and the restoration of the relationship, and the return of the person or the town to balance — by confession, by restitution, by reconciliation, or by cleansing.

4 And the order of the whole matter is this: afa reveals the imbalance; truth establishes the wrongdoing; justice corrects it; and cleansing restores the harmony. Four things, in that order, and each of them in its own hand. Afa is not a court, and the Dibia is not a judge, and no person is punished by a reading.

Chapter 7 — The Woman Who Kept Her Ground

A story of the purity code.

1 There was a woman in a certain town whose compound was the cleanest in the whole village — and she was not rich.

2 Every morning before the sun was high she swept. She swept the yard, and the path to the road, and the threshold of her husband's shrine. She washed the sill. She put out fresh water. She whitened the stone at the door with nzu.

3 And her neighbours laughed at her, saying: "What is a swept ground worth? Sweep it today and the dust returns tomorrow."

4 Now in that year there was a quarrel in the town, and a man was killed, and the elders said the ground was defiled. And every compound in the town was searched, for the elders said that where the defilement rested, there would be a sign.

5 And they came to her compound last, and there was no sign in it — no rubbish, no standing water, no trodden filth, nothing that the ground could hold against her.

6 And the elders said: "This woman's ground has nothing to say against her."

7 And the town was cleansed, and the ground of the people who had laughed at her was washed twice.

Chapter 8 — The Boundary Stone

A story of the law.

1 Two men were neighbours, and their farms met at a stone.

2 And the first man, wanting more land, moved the stone in the night — a little, and then a little more, until his neighbour's farm had lost the width of a whole ridge.

3 And the neighbour said nothing, and planted his yams, and they grew.

4 Now the first man's yams grew crooked and small, and his wife's cocoyam rotted in the ground, and his goats bore no young. And he said nothing to anyone, and he became thin.

5 And at the new moon he went to the diviner. And the diviner threw the chaplets and read them, and he did not speak for a long time. And then he said:

"The stone is not where your father set it."

6 And the man confessed. And the elders took the stone and put it back, and they measured the ridges with a cord, and the lost ground was returned.

7 And the elders said: "Now return the nights you stole." And he worked his neighbour's farm for a full planting season.

8 And his yams grew straight again.

Chapter 9 — The Man Who Would Not Be Cleaned

A story of the greater cleansing.

1 A man of a certain town killed a kinsman in anger, in a quarrel over a goat.

2 And the elders did the law: he was banished, and his family paid the blood-price, and he went away for seven years.

3 And at the end of the seven years he came back, and he did not come to be cleansed. He said the years had been enough, and he began to farm.

4 And in that season the rain came wrong. It fell on the farms of his neighbours and not on his. And the wells in his quarter began to dry. And the elders said: "Something on this ground is unfinished."

5 And the diviner was called, and he threw the chaplets, and he read the throw and then he threw again, and he read, and the reading was consistent, and it stood.

6 And he said: "There is a man in this quarter who was banished and who came back without being cleaned. The ground has forgiven nothing. It is only waiting."

7 And the man was brought, and he confessed before the whole quarter, not to the priest in secret but to everybody, for the wrong had been done to the ground the whole of them stand on.

8 And the cleansing was done: water was poured, nzu was applied, ogilisi was burned, white cloth was laid — and the community was present, and the man made restitution to the family a second time, and he kept the discipline of the clean ground for a full season without a single lapse.

9 And in the next season the rain came to his farm like anybody else's.

Chapter 10 — The Children of the Same Ground

A story of the assembly.

1 Two towns quarrelled over a stretch of land, and each said the land was its own.

2 And they took it to the Ikala, and the council sat, and they could not agree.

3 And the council said: "Bring the oldest person from each town, and let them speak — but let them speak last, after everyone else has spoken."

4 So the young men spoke first, and they were loud. And the elders of middle age spoke, and they were careful. And at the end the two oldest were brought in, and asked.

5 And the oldest of the first town said: "When I was a boy, my father took me to that land, and there was a stone there with the mark of our people on it."

6 And the oldest of the second town said: "When I was a boy, my father took me to that land, and there was a stone there with the mark of our people on it."

7 And both of them were telling the truth.

8 And the council said: "Then the stone has two marks, and the land belongs to the ground and not to us." And they set the boundary between the two claims, and gave the strip to neither town, and planted it, and neither town farmed it, and both towns kept the trees on it in common.

9 And the quarrel ended, and neither town lost face, for the assembly does not give a verdict — it restores a circle.

Chapter 11 — The Market of Dungs

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 The market of that town had gone bad, and the whole town knew it.

2 The young people laughed at it and called it the market of dungs. The old looked at it and saw a mark of decay, and remembered that the market had been great in the days of their youth.

3 And one of the old men said:

"Perhaps our neighbours are as corpses that do not feel pain when the worms eat them. It is for us to make them aware of the disgraceful condition of their market place."

4 And tens and tens of the villagers were taking oaths at a shrine close by that market. They swore, one after another, that they had not dropped the dungs there.

5 For the elders and the youths had met, in private, again and again, and had tried to find out the cause of their shame — and had failed. And they knew that their neighbours were laughing at the town.

6 And at last the tortoise's turn came.

7 Before the shrine he did what the others had done. He called the toll and the bell, and he put his question:

"Did I drop the dungs?"

8 And the alusi's guttural sounds came out of the shrine:

"They are Mbe's dungs!"

9 The people were furious. An old man sighed:

"There is no tale of shame without Mbe. Now, this farm day is lost to us."

10 And Mbe was thrown into a deep cesspit.

11 He stayed in it six days, and bore his punishment with great patience.

12 And on the seventh day, when the villagers came to pull him out, he kicked and shouted at them:

"Quickly! quickly! pull me up — quickly, it is stinking down here!"

BOOK III — Ndi Eri — The Book of the Ancestors

(Reincarnation, ancestral presence)

Chapter 1 — The Origin of the Ancestors (Mbido Ndi Eri)

1 When the first Mmadụ drew his final breath, Chukwu did not abandon him to the void. He took him to the threshold between Enu (Sky) and Ana (Earth) and made him the bridge. The ancestors are not dead; they are Ndi avuro anya (The Unseen Seen). They are the roots of the living tree; the tree does not grow tall without the roots in the dark soil. Every man walks upon the shoulders of his fathers. To disrespect an elder is to disrespect the root; to honour an elder is to water the root.

Chapter 2 — The Geography of Ana mmụọ (The Spirit-Land)

1 Ana mmụọ is a mirror of Uwa, but reversed. The sun sets where ours rises. Rivers flow upwards into the sky. The yams are made of light, not flesh. It is divided into three territories: 2 The Council-Hut of the Elders (Ụnọ Nzukọ Ndi Ichie): Where the great ancestors, warriors, Dibias, and Kings, sit in judgment and guide the living through dreams and omens. 3 The Periphery of Mists (Ọzala Mmụọ): Where the souls of the wicked, the cowardly, and the unbaptized wander, invisible to the council, waiting for a descendant to perform corrective rites (Iru Ana) so they may be summoned inward. 4 The Forest of Rebirth (Ọvịa Ilo Uwa): Where souls who are ready to return to Uwa gather. They choose their next body among their own descendants, waiting for the drum of childbirth to sound.

Chapter 3 — The Reading of the Ofo (Ịgụ Ofo)

1 When the soul enters the Spirit-Land, it comes before the Council of Seven Elders, the first ancestors of the seven clans. There, the soul places its Ofo before them. The Ofo is the witness of the life that was lived. It is not weighed against gold, stone, feather or any other object, for no external thing can measure a person's truth. The Ofo reveals what the person carried within their life. The Elders ask: “Gịnị ka i mee? Gịnị ka i ji? Gịnị ka ị lapụụ?” What did you do? What did you owe? What did you leave behind? They examine the person's deeds, their obligations to family and community, the oaths they kept or broke, the harm they caused, the good they created, and the consequences their life left upon people and Ana. For Ana does not count appearances; Ana reveals consequences. A person who lived imperfectly but recognised their wrongs, repaired what they could and restored what they damaged may find their Ofo made light. A person who appeared righteous while living through deceit, cruelty or exploitation may find their Ofo burdened. Then the ancestors break kola and ask: “Kee ive ị vụụ n’avịa?” What did you see in the marketplace?

2 For earthly life is the marketplace: a place where every person receives gifts, enters relationships, makes choices, assumes obligations and leaves something behind. The soul recounts its life, not only what it did, but what it learned and what became of its deeds. The Elders then determine its path. Those who are ready join the ancestors. Those whose wrongs remain unresolved enter the Periphery of Mists, where they confront what they have done and seek understanding and restoration. Others may return to the world of the living to complete an unfinished destiny. For in Odiana, judgement is not vengeance.

Chapter 4 — The Great Mandate of Rebirth (Iwu Ilo Uwa) — THE SACRED KEY

1 Hear this, O children of Ana: Reincarnation is not a possibility; it is a Covenant sealed by the soil. The gateway to rebirth is sealed by the soil of Ana. Without the Rite of the Seven Clods (Iru Ana), performed by a rightful elder (Onye Nze) over a body laid in ancestral ground, the soul is barred from reincarnation. It wanders the misty peripheries of Ana mmụọ, becoming a lost echo (Onye Nkpagbu) until a descendant performs the corrective burial. 2 The Requirement: The body must be washed with spring water (mmili iyi) infused with nzu (white chalk). It must be wrapped in a pure white wrapper (akwa ọcha). The grave must be dug facing East, towards Anyanwu. 3 The Rite of the Seven Clods: The elder drops seven clods of earth from the four corners of the compound and the three paths leading out of the village into the grave, chanting the seven sacred names of the ancestors of the land. Only then is the soul's name entered into the Mkpuru-Ndụ (Book of Life/Seed) of the lineage. 4 The Speed of Return: A warrior who dies defending his village reincarnates within a single generation (often as the first child born to his own son). A coward or a traitor waits twelve generations, watching his descendants prosper without him. A stillborn child reincarnates immediately into the next pregnancy of the same mother, for the soul merely touched the gate and returned to the forest to wait for a stronger vessel.

Chapter 5 — The Liturgy of Invocation (Ịkpọku Ndi Ichie)

1 At the New Moon, the Onye Ichie (family elder) cracks a kola nut (oji) at the family shrine (Okpensi), facing the Okpensi (ancestral altar). He calls out four names: his father, his grandfather, his great-grandfather, and the unknown first planter of the clan. He says: "Unu bịa lie nni, unu bịa nwụọ mmanya, unu bịa nye anyị ezi uche. Anyị bụ mkpụrụ unu; unu bụ mgbọlọgwụ anyị." (Come eat, come drink, come give us good counsel. We are your seeds; you are our roots). The spirits feast on the aroma; the living consume the flesh.

Chapter 6 — Obi Ike n'Ọnwụ (The Fearless Heart in Death)

1 Hear this, children of Chukwu: The body is not the self; it is the sheath of the knife. When the knife is drawn, the sheath is discarded. Do not mourn the sheath; wield the blade. When a man falls in battle, he does not vanish into silence. His mmuo obi (soul) rises instantly, not as a ghost, but as a traveller returning from a long journey. He is met at the boundary of Ana mmụọ by his Ndi Ichie (ancestors), who examine his hands. If they are stained with cowardice, he is sent to the periphery to wait. But if they are stained with the dust (nzu) of a righteous fight, he is led to the Great Council Hut, where he is given a seat. He rests, he eats, he strategises.

2 For the soul does not stay in Ana mmụọ forever; that land is a homestead, not a prison. When the time is right, when the planting season of destiny arrives, the soul chooses a new infant in its own lineage. It returns to Uwa (the Marketplace) to finish the work it began. Therefore, death is merely a rest between two labourers. Why fear a rest? Why cling to a sheath? -

3 Odiana’s own addition to this book:

Chapter 7 — Ebibi — the Market of the Soul

1 The world is a market. It gives equality of opportunity, and not equality of outcome. 2 A person who falls short in this life is not finished. He may negotiate a better standing for himself in the next cycle of reincarnation — and that is ebibi. 3 Retribution may be deferred to a third or a fourth return. 4 So no one should despair at the prosperity of the wicked, and no one should presume on the patience of Ana. The market opens again.

Chapter 8 — The Coward and the Brave

A story of the return.

1 Two men of the same lineage died on the same day — one in the defence of the town, and one running from the fight.

2 And the people buried them in the same ground, for both had been born of that lineage, and the rite was done for both.

3 But the tradition says what happened next.

4 The brave man was met at the boundary by his fathers, and they examined his hands, and the dust of the fight was on them, and he was given a seat in the great council hut.

5 And the coward was met too, and his hands were clean — and that was the trouble. For clean hands that have done nothing are not the same as hands that were never called. And he was sent to the mist to wait.

6 And the tradition says that in due season the brave man came back within a single generation — as the first son born to his own son, and they gave him the old man's name.

7 And the coward waited many generations, watching his descendants prosper without him, until a child was born in that house who was generous and brave, and it was him at last, and he had paid what he owed.

Chapter 9 — How Death Came to Be

A story of the council, and of the mercy that came with death.

1 In a time before the boundary between the body and the spirit was as firm as it is now, the elders of the communities met in a great market centre, to settle one matter: whether mankind should die.

2 They came from every place, and they filled the tiers of felled logs, and the latecomers stood. And there were elders among them, and titled people, and the leaders of the age grades, and the firstborn of families.

3 And two men walked into the sight of the assembly, and the talking stopped.

4 The first was a diviner. He wore a simple red cloth, and his eyes and his forehead and his feet were white with nzu. In his left hand he carried a divination bowl covered in raffia cloth, and he stood apart from the crowd, and the space around him stayed.

5 The second was a king of the earth — Ézè Anị. He wore a red woven cap with an eagle's feather at the side of it. Thin lines were cut diagonally across his forehead. He carried the ofo in his right hand, and he wore a long white shirt over a red wrapper that came to his knees. Cowry shells circled his wrists and his ankles, and strings of ivory beads hung at his neck, and each step he took was accompanied by the small clink of the shells.

6 And a woman came to him carrying a wooden plate of kola nuts, and a small bowl of palm wine. Her hair, her neck, her wrists and her feet were adorned with ropes of red coral. She gave him the plate and the bowl and stood at his side.

7 And Ézè Anị looked out at the gathered people, and seeing that he had them, he broke the kola.

8 And this is how he broke it. First he thanked Chukwu. Then he thanked Anị for her bounty, and Igwe for his rains, and Amadioha for his guidance and his discipline, and Ìfèjiọkụ for her harvest — and he made sure to name the alusi he had not named directly as well. And as he spoke he poured wine from a small calabash onto the ground.

9 Then he thanked the elders for coming. And he said:

"My people, I have a message for you. Do you want to hear it?"

10 And the assembly answered: "Tell us."

11 And Ézè Anị told them what had been revealed to him in the night. And it was the message of death.

12 And because the news was death, the people did not celebrate, and they went home.

13 And the next day they returned, and Ézè Anị broke the kola again, and he told them what Chukwu had added to the message — and this part is the mercy:

14 That from that day people would move between the world of the spirit and the world of the living. That when a person died he became a spirit. But that Chukwu had also listened to those who did not wish to remain spirits — and so spirits would be given the right to reincarnate.

15 And Anị, who makes the new souls and brings them into the world, would also receive the old souls at the end of their journey, and send them back again at the right time.

16 And that a person who had served the community well enough would become ichie — an honoured ancestor, even as a spirit — and those spirits would choose when, and whether, to come back at all, and would support their lineage from the spirit realm.

17 And when he had finished, Ézè Anị struck his ofo on the ground, and sealed the new ways.

18 And the elders went back to their communities and told the people, and their descendants after them.

Chapter 10 — Ọnwụ Ayolo, and the Voice in the Boundary

A story of the ancestors, and of a boundary shown out of Ana mmụọ.

1 There was an old man who had much land and no son.

2 And whenever he quarrelled with anybody he remembered it — that he had no child whose hand would eat his ekpe; and that his brothers would divide what he left, and there would be nobody to stand in his place. And every morning he took his ofo and blessed with it, and prayed to his chi to send him a child of his own hand, for he knew that the time of his death had come near.

3 And at last a daughter was born to him, and he named her Ọnwụ Ayolo.

4 And when she was twelve years old he gathered all his kinsmen, and he used one goat to settle Ọnwụ Ayolo in the word of the ancestors, so that she would hold his land for the husband who would come, as the custom required.

5 And it grieved his brothers greatly — the ones who had been waiting to eat his ekpe.

6 And he died one month after he had settled her.

7 And because Ọnwụ Ayolo did not know the boundaries of her many plots, one of her father's brothers — a very greedy man — began to take her land. Every year that passed he moved at the boundary of their land and gathered a little more of hers. And whenever she answered him, his children overpowered her.

8 And this kept grieving her father, where he was in Ana mmụọ.

9 And one afternoon, as she was coming home, her father called the other spirits and they went and hid themselves in the bush that was on the path she would take.

10 And when she came to that place she heard a voice like her father's voice, calling her. And it shook her. And the voice was singing:

Ọnwụ Ayolo, Ọnwụ Ayolo nwa m

Ọnwụ Ayolo

Ọ Ọnwụ Ayolo!

11 And the song went on, and it comforted her, and it named the ants' mound, and the trap that was made long ago, and the spear and the rest. And what it was telling her was where her father had hidden the marks of his boundary.

12 And she wept, and turned back, and went to look for them. And she found them — in the middle of that man's land.

13 And she came to that place again, and heard the voice again, and heard him sing it again. And now she knew for certain that it was her father, showing her the boundaries of her land.

14 And she went home in peace, and she went to the king and told him what that man and his kinsmen were doing to her.

15 And it grieved the king greatly to hear that not one person among her own kinsmen would show her the boundary of her land. And he told her to make her claim, and to recover every plot.

16 And the king called together the ndị ichie and all the elders of that town, and they sat to judge between them.

17 And before that day came, her kinsmen gathered and swore an oath among themselves that not one of them would show all the land her father had held.

18 And from that day, whenever she went to the king's house, her father was calling his fellow spirits to his house in the middle of the night, and singing the same song.

19 And on the day of the judgment, all the ndị ichie and all the elders gathered at Ọnwụ Ayolo's house, because they saw that her father had been the ọkpara — the firstborn — in that family. And while they were gathering she heard her father's voice calling her, and singing it again.

20 And when her kinsmen had said everything they had to say about the matter, she kept silent.

21 And when the king called on the man who was disputing with her to show where her boundary was when her father was alive, the man went and showed where he had heaped food in the ground. And when he was asked whether he would swear that what he was saying was true, he kept silent.

22 And when Ọnwụ Ayolo was called, she led them into the middle of the place where that man had stored his food, and showed them the ants' mound, and the spear, and the trap that were there. And she told them that she would swear whatever oath was brought to her.

23 And when the man was asked whether he would deny what the girl had said, he kept silent, because fear had taken him and his brothers.

24 And at last the great elder of that land stood up, and raised his ofo, and drew it across his eyes, and struck it on the ground. And he told them that he knew that boundary well, and that he had seen where Ọnwụ Ayolo had shown them, and that it was as it had been when her father was farming that land.

25 And the king stood up and announced that Ọnwụ Ayolo had won.

26 And he fined the man one goat, and four pots of palm wine, and a great fowl, and a large sum of money to be repaid to Ọnwụ Ayolo; and he gave the man a law to leave her all the land he had taken from her.

BOOK IV — The Book of Chi

(Personal destiny, inner self, spiritual agency)

Chapter 1 — The Origin of Chi (Mbido Chi)

1 As a single fire lights a thousand torches without diminishing itself, so Chukwu broke off a fragment of His own divine essence and placed it within the chest of every Mmadụ. This fragment is Chi. It is not a guardian angel; it is You, the eternal, individuated spark of the Supreme Light that existed before Ana and will exist after the stars cool. Your Chi is the captain of your ship; your body is the vessel; your mind is the compass.

Chapter 2 — The Dialogue with Chi (Mkparịtaụka Chi)

1 Every man walks with his Chi, but not every man listens. The Chi whispers; it does not shout. It nudges; it does not drag. When a man says, "Ekwere m" (I agree, aligned with my destiny), his Chi illuminates his path, and the doors of opportunity swing open. When a man says, "Ekwere m o" (I disagree, driven by fear or greed), his Chi retreats into silence, and the man becomes Onye Nkpagbu, a lost soul drifting by his ego, listening to the chaos of Ekwensu rather than the stillness of his own divine spark.

Chapter 3 — The Doctrine of Self-Mastery (Ịgba Chi)

1 To master the world, one must master the self. The three mortal enemies of the Chi are: 2 Anyaukwụ (Greed): The insatiable hunger for more land, more wealth, more wives. It blinds the eye to the needs of the neighbour. 3 Nganga (Pride): The arrogance that deafens the ear to the counsel of elders.
