It builds a house on sand. 4 Ụjọ (Fear): The paralysis that prevents the hand from planting the yam or lifting the spear. It is the opposite of faith. He who conquers these three sees his Chi clearly. He does not need divination to know his fate; he is his fate. He lives with the steady light of a lantern in a dark market, seeing clearly while others stumble.

Chapter 4 — The Liturgy of Alignment (Ịkpọ Chi)

1 Before the sun rises (tu Anyanwu ebili), the faithful face East, breathe deeply, and whisper: "Chi m, kpọte m. Ndu m, duga m. Anyanwu binie, ka m binie. Ọnwụ egburo m, maka na ị bụ ndụ m." (My Chi, wake me. My life, lead me. The Sun rises, let me rise. Death does not kill me, because you are my life.) He pours a libation of palm wine onto the ground for his Chi, not to worship it as a god, but to nourish the relationship, because even the divine spark requires the fuel of gratitude. This is the daily communion.

2 Odiana’s own addition to this book:

Chapter 5 — The Limit of the chi

1 And know this limit: a diviner may move mountains, and a healer may raise the sick, but when it comes to a person's own destiny, no one else can carry it. 2 You are the only one who can save yourself.

Chapter 6 — Ikenga, and the Hand

A story of the right hand.

1 A young man complained to a priest that his chi had deserted him, for everything he put his hand to had failed.

2 And the priest said: "Hold out your right hand." And the man held it out.

3 And the priest said: "What is in it?" And the man said: "Nothing."

4 And the priest said: "Then it is not your chi that has deserted you."

5 And the man was angry, and said: "I have asked my chi every morning, and it says nothing."

6 And the priest said: "Chi whispers. It does not shout. And it speaks to a hand that is working, not to a hand that is held out."

7 And the man went and cleared a farm.

Chapter 7 — The Orphan and His Father's Wife

A folktale of the Igbo, read in the law.

1 There was a boy whose mother died, and whose father took another wife.

2 And the woman hated the boy, because he was not hers, and she gave him the smallest share and the heaviest work. And she sent him to the stream for water at dusk, when the path is dark, and she sent him to the forest for firewood in the rain.

3 And the boy did everything he was told, and swept the compound, and said nothing.

4 And he sang while he worked. And the song he sang is remembered:

"Rachaa wọọ nwa enwe nne nda" — and the other children mocked him for it.

5 Now it happened that a famine came, and the woman's own son fell sick, and no medicine in the town would serve. And the elders said: "A child is dying, and there is a thing that must be done, and it must be done by a child of that house who has a clean hand."

6 And not one of the woman's own children had a hand clean enough, for they had learned their mother's manner, and their hands were full of snatching.

7 And the boy who swept — who had been given the least and had taken nothing — was the only one whose hand was clean.

8 And he did what was needed, and the other child lived.

9 And when the woman saw it she sat down on the ground and covered her head, and she said: "I gave him the least, and he gave my son his life."

BOOK V — The Book of Agwu

(Mystery, intuition, divination, madness, creativity)

Chapter 1 — Agwu as the Radiant Knowledge (Agwu Ọmamihe)

1 Agwu is not the spirit of madness. Agwu is the spirit of skill, high intuition, and cosmic creativity. He is the ancient tongue of the universe that teaches the blacksmith how to temper steel, the carver how to release the spirit trapped in the wood, and the diviner how to read the whispers of Ana. In the traditions of the East, Agwu is the clear light of the mind unclouded by desire. He is the sharp edge of the knife that distinguishes truth from illusion. When Agwu visits a man, the man does not babble or tear his clothes; rather, he becomes eerily calm, hyper-observant, and speaks in sharp, cryptic clarity. He is an Onye Nkà (the skilled one).

Chapter 2 — The Gifts of Agwu (Onyinye Agwu)

1 Agwu bestows four sacred gifts upon his chosen: 2 Awakening (Ọkwụ Agwu): A sudden, intense clarity about the nature of existence, often during meditation or deep isolation in the forest. 3 The Healing Hand (Aka Ọgwụ): Knowing exactly which root and leaf to combine to cure a fever or heal a wound, without being taught by any mortal master. 4 The Seeing Eye (Anya Afa): The ability to see the inner and direct cause of a physical ailment or community conflict. 5 The Tongue of Parable (Ire Amamife): The ability to speak in proverbs that cut through lies and confusion, revealing the core truth of a matter instantly.

Chapter 3 — The Call of the Dibia (Priesthood Mandate)

1 The Dibia is not a man who seeks spirits; he is a man sought by the clan. By sacred law, the priesthood is not hereditary. The novice undergoes a rigorous 12-year seminary (Uko-Ndose), modelled on the great seminaries of the Catholics but rooted in the tradition. He learns: 2 The 16 signs of Afa and their 256 permutations. 3 The medicinal properties of all leaves and roots of the forests of the land. 4 The strict code of hygiene and ritual cleanliness (he must wash three times a day, keeping his body, his robes, and his shrine immaculate). 5 The art of silence and dignified presence. A Dibia does not run, shout, or dance chaotically; he moves like the great python of Idemmili, deliberately, silently, and with terrible purpose.

Chapter 4 — The Liturgy of the Dibia's Consecration

1 The new Dibia kneels before the Ika Mmuo (High Priest). The Ika Mmuo places an eagle feather (Ugo) into the Dibia's hair and whispers: "Ị bụzi oche Agwu. Eziokwu ka ị ya na-ekwu, n'agbanyei na a ya-ata gi ụta. Ọbala adina na aka gị; ntu adina gị na ire." (You are now the seat of Agwu. Truth you speak, even if it brings bitterness. No blood stains your hands; no falsehood stains your tongue). The Dibia rises, takes his staff (Ofo), and is given a new Afa Uchu, a secret name known only to him and his Chi.

Chapter 5 — The Diviner Who Sent Them Home

A story of the judgment of a reading.

1 A family came to a diviner about a sickness, and the diviner prepared the session: he received them, he shared the kola, he called on Chukwu, he took the fee, he blew his horn, he marked the ground with white chalk, and he took up the chaplets.

2 And he threw, and he read, and he did not like what he read.

3 For the question was about the sick child, and the signs that came were about a journey and a market debt — and neither of them had anything to do with the child.

4 So he blew his horn and sang the praise of Agwu, for lying, and he threw again.

5 And the signs came out the same.

6 And the diviner put the chaplets down, and said to the family:

"Agwu is lying today. I will not read for you from a lying mouth. Go home, and come back on another

day."

7 And the family were angry, and said they had paid.

8 And he gave the fee back.

9 And on the eighth day they came again, and he prepared the session again, and he threw, and the reading matched the question, and he answered it, and the child was treated and lived.

Chapter 6 — The One the Diviners Could Not Read

The story of Udenolu, who became Ézè Anị.

1 Once, in a place called Amambi, a spirit was born as flesh.

2 He was born on the night the sky swallowed the moon — and on such a night the line between the world of man and the world of the spirit is thin and nothing holds it, and as his body was forming, a spirit latched on to it and changed him for ever.

3 So he was neither man nor woman, and neither living nor dead.

4 And the people tried to fit him into their society, and he knew that he did not fit. He grew up lost. He did not farm, and he did not tap wine, and he did not start a trade. He spoke of spirits, and of creatures that no one else could see. He was troubled by dreams, and sometimes he woke the household with his screams.

5 And most of the people called him strange, because they did not understand him; and they called him lazy, because he did not add to what the community had. And they did their best to avoid him.

6 And his family called the diviners.

7 And the diviners consulted Chukwu for him — and they came back without an answer, every one of them.

8 But there was one person in that household who did not avoid him, and she fed him, and she talked with him by the fire, and she worked with him in the garden. And her name was Nné.

9 Now in time Nné's body did not house her spirit any more, and she died. And Udenolu found her, and informed her family and the people of Amambi. And as the closest living person to her, the duty of her burial fell to him.

10 And he cried. He cried with the diviners who came to hold him up while her body was lowered into the ground and covered with earth.

11 And he knew what the law knows — that the world does not belong to any person permanently, and that any time in this realm is a gift — and he knew that her soul had gone on to the next stage of its journey.

12 And he cried anyway, and he did not want the tears to stop, for the tears carried all the love she had given him.

13 And then the people of Amambi prepared to send off her spirit to the ancestral realm.

14 And although Nné had no living relatives, her send-off was one of the biggest that Amambi had ever seen. The people came with cowry and with precious stones. And one of the famous blacksmiths of Ọka — the best in the whole land — presented a bronze statue of a vulture.

15 And the people ate, and played music, and danced, and told the stories of Nné.

16 And at the centre of it all was Udenolu.

17 For by then he was Ézè Anị — the king of the earth — and it was he who presided over the ceremony, and it was he who shared the stories of Nné that nobody else knew.

18 And while he spoke with the people, the spirits came in to join them. Drawn by the merriment and by the new death, the wandering spirits filled the cleared space. And he saw Nné arrive. She danced with the dancers and ate from the tables of others, and she did it laughing.

19 And out of the corner of his eye he saw the ground open. He heard voices and laughter, and if he concentrated he could even smell the food and the wine. The elders of the spirit world had heard the celebration, and they were making ready for a new ancestor.

20 And Nné turned and smiled at him.

21 And he knew that she had seen him all along.

22 Then she fell, and returned to the world of the spirits. The ground closed, and nobody else seemed to have noticed.

23 And Udenolu stood looking at the place that had been a doorway only a moment before.

24 And when she fell, it looked like she was flying.

Chapter 7 — Arobinagu, the One Who Lives in the Wilderness

1 Agwu is the source, and Arobinagu is the first thing that comes out of it. And the religion keeps the two apart, as a river is kept apart from its spring.

2 Arobinagu is called the first son of Agwu. He is not Agwu, and he is not set beside Agwu. He is an emanation, and a focused expression, and Agwu remains the source.

3 And his names say where he is. Aho is the force, and bi is to dwell, and n'agu is in the wilderness — Ahobinagu, that which lives in the wilderness. And Obinagu is read as obi and n'agu: the heart of the forest.

4 And so he is the chi of the forest, and the keeper of its memory, and the oracle of the life that was never farmed.

5 And the forest, agu, is not waste ground. It is a realm of raw life, and a place of mystery and of change, and the one place where the order of men meets an intelligence that is not theirs. A person enters the forest as a guest who was not invited.

6 And therefore the religion keeps the Nso of the forest. No one clears the grove that has been left standing; no one takes from the forest in greed; and no one enters it loudly. What is taken from agu is taken at its edge and in need, and what is left standing is left standing on purpose.

7 And Arobinagu is not to be called upon for small things — not for a debt, nor for a quarrel, nor for gain in the market. He is approached where the forest is, and for what the forest holds: healing that was not taught, and knowledge that was not read, and the fear that keeps a man honest about how little he knows.

8 And the religion says plainly what the two are, since people confuse them: Agwu is the broad field, and Arobinagu is one thing within it. Agwu is expansive; Arobinagu is particular. To use one name for the other is to confuse a river with its spring, and the practitioners of old did not do it.

Chapter 8 — Nne Agwu, Oke Agwu, and Ebo Agwu

1 And Agwu is known to the religion under three forms, and they are one thing seen from three sides.

2 Nne Agwu is the whole of it — the mother-form, and the intelligence behind insight, and craft, and intuition, and the waking of a person to what he is for. She is called the totality-sum, for nothing lies outside her.

3 And she is named first when the religion speaks of a gift that was never taught. An idea arrives whole, and the person did not build it. The hands know what the mind was never told. The dream gives the answer the day could not reach. And the person asks himself, "where did this come from?" and has no answer — and the having-no-answer is part of it.

4 And these are the signs that Nne Agwu is at work in a person, and the religion gives them, and then gives a warning with them.

5 The ideas do not stop. They come in a hard year, and in tiredness, and when the person is not even trying.

6 There is no Dibia in the family, and yet the faculties are already awake — an eye that knows before the event; dreams that are clear and mean something; a reading of people and of situations that nobody taught; a hand that finds the right leaf. And this confuses a person at first, for he has no lineage to explain it by.

7 And this is the doctrine the religion draws from it: Nne Agwu calls a person directly, and does not need a house to call through. So no one is turned away from a calling for want of a Dibia in his line — and the religion says so in law, and not as comfort.

8 And the warning, which is part of the doctrine and not a footnote to it. None of these signs is a licence. They do not make a person an authority, and they do not excuse him from learning, and they are not a mastery that arrived whole. What is truly from Nne Agwu produces self-forgetfulness, and discipline, and curiosity. What produces a swollen self, and no work, and no study, is not her.

9 And what a person who has recognised the signs is to do is not to announce it. It is to align — to learn more, and to watch himself, and to keep his discipline.

10 Oke Agwu is the same Agwu turned outward — the agency of it: the intelligence that sees what could be, and reaches for it, and chooses what it needs, and brings it into being. It does not mean a man, and the old teachers said so plainly: what is called masculine here is the activity, and not the sex.

11 And Ebo Agwu is Agwu particular — the form it takes in one person, and in one house, and in one work. So Nne Agwu is the whole and Ebo Agwu is the part, and a person lives inside the part.

12 And the religion holds the names together and makes no rank of them. A woman is not nearer to Nne Agwu for being a woman, and a man is not nearer to Oke Agwu for being a man. The one is the whole and the other is the going-out, and every person carries both and works with both.

Chapter 9 — Ara Agwu, the Disorder of the Gift

1 And Agwu can be disordered, and the disorder is called Ara Agwu. It is not a possession, and it is not an unclean thing that has got into a person. The religion teaches that it is the misalignment of a gift — and this is the whole of the doctrine, and all the rest is description.

2 And afa explains how a gift goes wrong. Aka Ose is the right way round: the wide memory that holds what has been done and known, and out of which a person draws. Ose Aka is the same thing turned: the channel distorted, so that what is sent through it is unstable, and broken, and not to be trusted.

3 And the religion says it in one line: the same channel that carries wisdom carries confusion when it loses its footing. So the disorder is not the arrival of a stranger. It is intelligence out of true.

4 And the marks of it are not the marks people expect. They look for a man raving in the market. The old teachers looked for the quiet failures.

5 Oseaka — the one who cannot keep what he receives. Money and favour come to him easily and leave as easily — and it is not generosity, and it is not the enjoyment of life. It is a repeated inability to keep what he has been given, an imbalance between receiving and stewarding. And the work set for him is not more abundance. It is discipline.

6 The one whose gift has come away from truth. He is a storyteller, and a good one; then the story becomes exaggeration, and the exaggeration becomes invention, and at last he tells the false thing where there was no reason to. And the religion's reading is this: the gift is not the problem. The absence of discipline is the problem. Directed into work, and into truth, and into service, the same gift is a blessing.

7 The one who cannot care for himself. The small tasks become too much; the body is neglected; the room falls into disorder; and the strength to look after himself is never there. And the religion says: caring for the body is not separate from caring for the spirit. The body is one of the first places where a man's balance, or his imbalance, becomes visible.

8 And near-success, which is the cruellest of them. A brilliant beginning, and an enthusiasm that carries others, and fast progress — and then he stops, and the work is never finished, and the pattern repeats for years. Beginnings are easy for him and completion is hard. And the reading is that his gift has not been ordered, and not that it is small. What turns a gift into a destiny is consistency.

9 And the religion's word on all of them together, and it is one word for each: every one of these qualities becomes a strength when it is cultivated, and every one of them is a burden when it is left alone. And the invitation is always the same — to bring the gift into balance.

10 And now the religion's plain warning, which it will not leave out of this chapter. These things have many causes, and most of them are not spiritual. A person who cannot sleep, and cannot keep money, and cannot finish his work may be sick, or grieving, or badly taught, or in a hard year — and he must be seen by those who know the body and the mind. A reading of afa is not a diagnosis, and no Dibia of this religion may treat it as one, and no one may be told that his sickness is his spirituality.

11 And the religion forbids the reading of every trouble as Agwu. Sometimes a man is tired because he has not slept. Sometimes a marriage is failing because nobody is talking. Sometimes a business is failing because the numbers do not work. And a Dibia who reads Agwu into all of it has stopped being useful.

12 And it is not to be named over a person lightly. "Do not label yourself," the old teachers said — and the religion makes it law.

Chapter 10 — The Aligning of Agwu

1 And the religion says the aligning of Agwu is simpler than people make it, and that it is not a matter of many rites. There are no endless ceremonies here, and no hunting for signs, and no drama. And the first question is not "what does Agwu want of me?" It is: what am I doing with what I have already been given?

2 And these are the works of the aligning.

3 Do the work that is in front of you. Not the thinking about it, nor the preparing for it, nor the talking about what will be done — the doing of it. Purpose becomes clearer by being practised. And a man may spend years asking Agwu to show him his path while stepping over the work already lying at his feet.

4 Learn something every day, and do not limit it to sacred things. Read, and study, and observe, and ask; learn the craft; learn the history of the family; learn from those who know more. And if the work needs the market, learn the market. Agwu and ignorance must never become comfortable together. A spirituality that leaves a person less able to deal with the world has been misunderstood.

5 Keep your own Nso. For where experience has shown a man, again and again, that a thing throws him out of true, the work is to stop negotiating with himself about it. Boundaries protect what is valuable, and the river is strong because it has banks.

6 And keep a quiet time, and keep it daily. Sit; let the breathing settle; let the thoughts settle; greet Agwu; watch what rises without answering it at once; and then go back to the day. Consistency matters more than performance. And over years a person learns to tell apart what is intuition, and what is fear, and what is impulse, and what is only his own wish talking.

7 Keep the body in good condition. Move it, and rest it, and feed it, and keep it clean. The body is the instrument by which a person does his work in this world — and a strong spirituality inside a neglected body is a contradiction the religion does not accept.

8 And study both sides of your ancestry — the mother's line and the father's line, and never one of them only. What gifts keep appearing? Healers, traders, farmers, teachers, artists, priests, craftsmen, leaders, musicians; and the ones known for judgement, or for courage, or for the telling of stories. And not every ancestral gift looks spiritual: a grandmother's gift for trade is a gift, and a grandfather's knowledge of plants is a gift.

9 And keep reverence for the forces that came before. Learn their names where they are known; keep their stories; speak well of those who lived honourably; and carry forward what was good in them. And the reverence shows in how a person lives — the greatest offering to the ancestors is to become a descendant worth having.

10 And the test, which the religion gives so that a person may judge himself. Aligning with Agwu produces something: more discipline, and more knowledge, and greater care, and better character, and clearer boundaries, and more useful work, and a firmer hold on what he is for. And if years of talk about Agwu leave a man less disciplined, and less useful, and less curious, and less steady than he was, then what he has been calling alignment should be looked at again.

11 Agwu is not an excuse for avoiding life. Rightly cultivated, it makes a person better at living it.

12 And Ulu Agwu is the shadow side of a gift, and the religion names it so that people stop being surprised by it. Where an ability has a strong and useful face, there is a drag and a difficulty that comes with it and demands attention. So a person should know what brings him back to himself, and make room for quiet before exhaustion makes it for him, and keep a boundary.

13 And the discernment here is plain: not every inconvenience is opposition. Sometimes a man is tired because he has not slept, and sometimes a relationship is failing because of how he speaks in it. And the aim of all of it is that a person become difficult to surprise — in himself.

14 And the religion keeps Ikpe Agwu, the refusing of the calling. A person may refuse the work, and refuse it in the open, before the Dibia and the Ndose, and the refusal is written down. And the religion does not hold him in contempt for it, and does not pursue him. But the religion says what the old teachers said: what is refused is not thereby removed. A gift refused does not go away. It goes sour. And the one who refuses is not punished for it; he lives without the thing he was for, and the religion says so once, and then lets him alone.

15 And the religion's duty of writing belongs to this book more than to any other. Knowledge that is never written down is at the mercy of memory, and memory dies. A Dibia who teaches ten apprentices touches ten lives. A Dibia who writes it down begins a conversation with people not yet born. So the religion charges its Dibia to write: the record, the reading, the case, the commentary, the dictionary, the translation.

16 And its boundary is kept also. Not everything sacred is to be published — for a tradition with no boundaries has nothing it can protect. But secrecy must not become the way a knowledge quietly dies out.

17 And the charge to the reader of this book, in the old words of the teachers:

"Rụọ ọrụ gị. Mụta ihe kwa ụbọchị. Kwanyere Nso gị ùgwù. Mee oge nke ịdị jụụ. Wusie ahụ gị ike. Mara onyinye ndị na-abịa site n'akụkụ abụọ nke ndị nna gị. Nọgide na-asọpụrụ ndị bu gị ụzọ. Na karịa ihe niile, zụlite Agwu gị nke ọma."

Do your work. Learn something every day. Honour your Nso. Keep a time of quiet. Strengthen your body. Know the gifts that come through both sides of your ancestry. Remain reverent toward those who came before you. And above all, cultivate your Agwu with care.

BOOK VI — The Book of Afa

The sixteen signs, the throw, the reading, and the judgment of a reading.

Chapter 1 — What afa is

1 Ana is the law. The community and the spirits enforce it. And afa is how the will of Chukwu is known among men. 2 Agwu does not be afa. Agwu reveals through afa. 3 The diviner does not guess and he does not invent. He asks, he throws, he reads, and he answers what was asked.

Chapter 2 — The chaplets

1 The instrument is a pair of chaplets. 2 Each chaplet is four seeds, strung together. 3 Every seed has two faces, one hollow and one rounded. When it falls, one face is upward. 4 A seed that falls hollow-side up is OPEN. A seed that falls rounded-side up is CLOSED. 5 Four seeds give sixteen dispositions. Two chaplets thrown together give 16 × 16, which is 256.

Chapter 3 — The preparation of a session

1 The clients are received in the Ndose. 2 Kola is offered and shared. 3 The diviner calls on Chukwu to send his blessing, and he refers to the reason they have come before they have stated it. 4 The eldest of the clients states the matter, and pays the token fee, placing it on the ground before the diviner. 5 The diviner blows his horn. 6 White chalk is given, and the diviner marks the ground with it. 7 He takes up the chaplets, and the reading begins.

Chapter 4 — The throw and the read

1 One chaplet in each hand, thrown forward, so that they lie parallel. 2 The two chaplets are read together, and they are read from the right to the left — not as writing is read. 3 Each disposition is a word, and the pair is a sentence. Two words from one throw. 4 And the words compound, and the order of the compounding is the meaning: the same two signs, reversed, are two different words.

Chapter 5 — The method

1 The diviner asks, then throws, then reads, then speaks, and the answer raises the next question. 2 He does not throw once. He throws twenty times and more, and each throw answers the question he put before it. 3 When a sign calls for praise, he recites the praise song to the alusi named, and then he throws again. 4 And when the reading is finished he stops. There is no padding, and there is no second reading to soften the first.

Chapter 6 — The judgment of a reading

1 Every sign carries a dominant theme. 2 The diviner shall test whether the themes he has thrown match the theme of the question asked. 3 If they do not match, Agwu is lying. Then the diviner blows his horn and sings the praise of Agwu for lying, and the lie is stopped. 4 And if Agwu continues to lie, the diviner shall end the session and send the client home, to come back another day. 5 A reading that does not answer the question is not a reading, and the diviner says so. This is the law of the diviner's honesty, and it is not to be set aside.

Chapter 7 — What may not be done

1 A reading is not sold twice. A question answered is answered; to ask again for a better answer is to invite the lie. 2 A diviner shall not speak openly of what he reads. 3 And no diviner shall prescribe the killing of anything. Where the old reading said make a blood sacrifice, the reading stands and the remedy is the oblation — kola, nzu, palm wine, and a cleansing.

Chapter 8 — Afa and moral disorder

1 When afa is consulted about a wrong — a quarrel, a harm, an obligation broken — the signs are read as showing harmony or imbalance. They are not proof of guilt. 2 The reading may point to deceit, or to injustice, or to an obligation not met, or to harmful conduct, or to a conflict that was never settled, or to the need for cleansing. It points. It does not convict. 3 And the diviner shall read the signs alongside the facts of the matter. The ground, the witnesses, the accounts of the people — the stones are read with the case in the hand, and never instead of it. 4 Where the wrong is established, the remedy is not punishment but repair: the harm corrected, the relationship restored, and the person or the community returned to balance — by confession, by restitution, by reconciliation, and by cleansing. 5 And the whole of the law is in one line, and it is to be kept: Afa reveals imbalance; truth establishes the wrong; justice corrects it; purification restores harmony. 6 So afa may never be used to convict a person. A community that takes a sign for a verdict has abandoned the ground and the witnesses — and the religion holds that the sign has then been used to do the very thing it exists to uncover.

Chapter 9 — Oru, and the Horn That Killed and Raised

A story of Ana mmụọ, and of the horn that was broken.

1 The king of Iduu had a son who was very headstrong. He did not listen to his mother or his father, and they warned him not to go out to the open ground when the cry came out — and he would not hear it.

2 And one spirit had it for its work to watch over Nwaimo at all times, and that spirit hated the duty, for it could never leave him.

3 And one afternoon, when the cry came out, Nwaimo answered it — "O! O! O!" — as if somebody were calling him. And he jumped over the wall of their compound and flew like a hawk to the ground where the dances were held. And Oru ran after him, calling him, warning him to come back.

4 And when they got there an old woman came out and said: "Children, little children, have pity on me and help me carry my firewood." And Oru looked, and saw that there was something wrong with that woman, and told her that they were going home to eat. And Nwaimo cut him short and said: "Do not mind her; we have eaten; bring the firewood and I will carry it for you."

5 And as soon as the firewood touched her head she set off for her house, and she was going very fast. And Oru came behind them quietly.

6 And they passed place after place, and when night was falling they came to that old woman's house. And her face was worse than a face should be.

7 And she said to them: "Go and fetch water — and do not come into the bedroom." And she pointed them to where the moon lived.

8 And Nwaimo went to fetch the water. And Oru went to the house of Ọnwa.

9 And as Oru was carrying leaves into Ọnwa's house he heard Ọnwa saying: "Hm, hm — a human smells." And Oru answered: "It is me. I do not know where I am. Please help me."

10 And Ọnwa had pity on him where he stood, and told him that he was in Ana mmụọ, the land of the spirits. And she told him that that woman was a wicked spirit, who was to be avoided, and that her name was bad for eating people. And she told him how to escape.

11 And Oru thanked her and went back.

12 And Oru came in at the head of the woman's house, and she seized him and asked him where he was, and what he was doing, going about the land. And Oru answered her nothing, and went and lay down on one side of the house, turning over in his mind what he would do in the night.

13 And after a while the woman brought them pounded yam and cooked cocoyam. And Oru told Nwaimo with his eyes not to eat it. And Nwaimo would not look at him, and ate it all, and asked her for more. And Oru did not touch it.

14 And at night the woman laid mats for them. And Oru lay down and pretended that sleep had taken him.

15 And Ọnwa came and struck the woman on the heart, and she slept.

16 And Oru opened his eyes and saw it, and quietly woke Nwaimo and put one hand over his mouth, and carried him out of that house. And the two of them ran for their lives.

17 And the woman slept her fill and woke and took up her whip and struck where the children had been lying, and it fell on nothing. And she took up her spirit horn and blew this song:

Opi ititiriri, opi ititiriri, tụgbuo Nwaimo

Ọ riri ji mmụọ

Ọ riri ede mmụọ

Tụgbuo ya

Tụgbuo ya

18 And Nwaimo fell down on the road and died.

19 And because Oru had not eaten that food, nothing touched him.

20 And Oru looked for a way to bring Nwaimo back, and everything he tried failed. And after a while the woman came out, and Oru hid behind a tree.

21 And the woman looked about her and saw that she had left her knife and her basket behind, and she ran back to fetch them — and she left her horn lying there.

22 And Oru came out from where he was watching, and took up the horn, and sang:

Opi ititiriri, opi ititiriri, tute Nwaimo

Ọ righi ji mmụọ

Ọ righi ede mmụọ

Tute ya

Tute ya

23 And Nwaimo rose up and was alive, and the two of them ran.

24 And the woman came back and found that they had gone, and she sang with her other horn again, and Nwaimo fell down dead again. And Oru brought him up again with the horn he had. And so it went, all the way home — the woman killing him with a song and Oru raising him with a song, and the two of them running.

25 And they reached home.

26 And the king made a great feast for them. And the people rejoiced that the son they had given up for dead was standing among them. And while they ate and made merry, everybody forgot Oru. There was not one person who remembered him — and some of them looked at him sideways and spoke to him with contempt.

27 And Oru remembered what he could do. He took up that horn and sang the song that kills, and he fell down dead in the middle of the feast.

28 And fear took hold of everybody. There was uproar, and people looked at one another with suspicion. And the king believed that everyone there knew what had happened to his son, and he made a law that nobody should leave his house until they had gone to afa.

29 And the afa threw, and it asked the king:

"Oru saved Nwaimo out of Ana mmụọ and brought him back from death and brought him to your house. What did you do for him?"

30 And when the king heard it he called Oru and told him to ask for whatever he needed, and it would be done for him. And Oru told the king what was owing to him, and the king gave him a great place in his house.

31 And then Oru took up that horn and raised Nwaimo, and he lived again.

32 And they broke that horn, so that Oru could not use it to kill Nwaimo again.

Chapter 10 — Ululu and Ete, and the Order of the Two

1 In afa two signs are read against each other, and the whole of their teaching lies in their order. They are Ululu and Ete. Change the order and the meaning turns over; that is how afa teaches.

2 Ululu is the body, and weight, and the thing that anchors. It is what holds a person to the ground and to the world he stands in. And nothing stands in this world without weight.

3 Ete is the bridge — the rope thrown across, the crossing, and the movement by which a person goes beyond where he is standing. The pathway, and the thing that makes a pathway possible at all.

4 And the religion says of the two: neither is evil and neither is holy. Both are given. So the question is never which of the two a person has. It is always which of the two leads.

5 Ululu Ete — the weight first, and the bridge after it. And this is the reading of a setback: pain, and delay, and tears (Anya Mmiri), and a life that grows heavier the further it goes.

6 And the meaning of it is plain. When the body governs everything, the crossing is dragged. The bridge is still there — but it is being carried by the weight, and a bridge that is carried cannot do the work of a bridge.

7 And the marks of Ululu Ete are these: the craving leading, and the comfort deciding, and the fear choosing, and the short thing taken in the place of the long thing. And a man who knows the better road and does not take it is reading this sign in his own life.

8 Ete Ululu — the bridge first, and the weight after it. And this is the reading of the fast. For Ibu Onu is nothing else: the bridge set in front, and the body behind it.

9 And what comes out of Ete Ululu is not the destruction of the body. The religion does not teach that the body is the enemy of the person who has it. It teaches that a body which leads is a body out of place, and that a body in its place is the best servant a person will ever have.

10 So the correction of a setback is not the overthrow of the body but the turning round of the order — Ululu Ete turned into Ete Ululu. The disorder was never in the body. The disorder was in the order.

11 And the sign carries one thing more, and the religion keeps it. Ete Ululu is also the sign of receptivity, and of carrying — of the one who empties in order to receive, and withdraws in order to make. And the religion names women in that correspondence, and honours it, and does not make it small. But it binds the fast on no one by sex: the emptying that makes room is the shape of the practice itself, and every person who fasts does it.

12 And the religion's word on hearing chi: the noise of appetite is not a voice. A person who has never once set the body behind him has never yet heard what stands in front of him.

13 And whoever is given this reading is given no penance with it. A reading is a diagnosis, and the cure is the order of his own days. So the Dibia who reads Ululu Ete says what he sees, and hands the person his life back.

BOOK VII — The Book of Amadioha

(Moral, spiritual, and community laws)

Chapter 1 — The Law of Restitution (Nkwụghachi)

1 Justice is not about revenge; it is about restoring the broken circle of the community. 2 Theft: If a man steals a goat, he returns four goats. If he steals a cow, he returns four cows, and anything a man steals, he returns it times four. 3 Injury: If a man breaks another man's arm, his own arm is not broken in return. Instead, he must work the victim's farm for a full planting season, providing his labour as the cure. 4 Murder: The murderer does not die (for blood calls blood, creating an endless cycle). Instead, he is banished from the village (Ipu n'Obodo) for seven years. His family must pay the Iwu (Blood-Price) of 30 cows and a plot of prime farmland to the victim's family. If he refuses, Amadioha will strike his household with lightning until the debt is settled.

Chapter 2 — The Law of the Assembly (Otu Ọraeze)

1 No man is a king over his own judgment. All major disputes, land division, marriage rights, title-taking- must be brought to the Otu (Village Assembly) under the sacred Oji tree. No decision is valid unless 49 elders (7 x 7, the number of divine completion) agree. The minority, even if wrong, must be heard for three days; for truth often comes from the quietest voice, and Ekwensu speaks loudest in the majority.

Chapter 3 — The Law of War (Iwu Agha)

1 War is a last resort, a bitter medicine, permitted only for: 2 Defence of the borders of Ana: If a foreigner (Oji Okpolo) shifts the sacred boundary stones of the land. 3 Rescue of a captured kinsman: If a child is taken into slavery. 4 Atonement for a broken treaty: If a neighbouring clan violates a sworn blood-pact. Before war, a white fowl is sacrificed to Amadioha at the Ndose (Temple). The Dibia reads the fowl's entrails: 5 If the liver is spotted, the war is cursed; do not proceed. 6 If the liver is pure white, the battle is blessed. Strike fast, strike true, and return before the sun sets on the third day. The warrior who falls in righteous war is guaranteed a seat in the Council-Hut of Elders and a rebirth within a single season.

Chapter 4 — The law of ownership (Iwu Ohu)

1 No person is another person's property.

2 No member of Odiana shall hold a human being as property, nor buy one, nor sell one, nor carry one in a ship or on a road, nor stand surety for such a trade.

3 And no person shall be brought into a Ndose against his will.

4 And the law is not new in spirit. "Our own law held that a slave is a human being who must not be killed, at a time when European slavers were killing slaves." The old law reached as far as forbidding the killing. Odiana forbids the holding.

5 And the religion reads the older law as an admission and not as a permission. A rule against killing a thing is proof that the thing was there — so the religion goes further than the old law, and says that it has gone further.

6 And this is the law of the religion and not of any state. Where the law of a land permits what this law forbids, the member of Odiana is bound by this law, and answers for it at the Ndose.

Chapter 5 — The Secret Confession (Nchegharị)

1 When a person carries guilt for a wrong committed, they may privately seek the Nze of Nchegharị, the keeper of confession. The meeting is held in secret, away from the shrine and the community, and the Nze is bound to silence. The person confesses truthfully what they have done, without fear of public shame. The Nze listens, questions where necessary, and reminds them of the obligations they have broken before Ana, their Chi, and their people. Confession does not erase the consequences of wrongdoing. Where another person has been harmed, the Nze may require restitution, reconciliation, service, or another act appropriate to the wrong. Where restitution would endanger the innocent or expose a victim to further harm, the Nze must seek a safer path. When the person has sincerely accepted their wrongdoing and undertaken what is required of them, the Nze gives Nchegharị, declaring the person's path open again: “Ana anụla gị. I kwuola eziokwu. Gbanwee obi gị, dozie ihe ị mebiri, jee n’udo.” Ana has heard you. You have spoken the truth. Change your heart, repair what you have damaged, and go in peace. The confession remains between the person and the Nze. No priest may use what is confessed for personal advantage, public humiliation, revenge, or gossip. For Nchegharị is not the hiding of wrongdoing; it is the beginning of making right what has been made wrong. The person leaves without the burden of secrecy, but with the responsibility of transformation.

Chapter 6 — The Tortoise and the Goat

A folktale of the Igbo, read in the law.

1 The goat and the tortoise were friends, and they agreed to make a farm together.

2 The goat cleared the bush, and the tortoise carried the seed. The goat dug the ridges, and the tortoise carried the water. And when the harvest came, the goat said:

"I cleared and I dug. The yam is mine."

3 And the tortoise said nothing, and went home.

4 Now the goat ate his yams, and ate them all, and made a great feast, and invited the town — and he did not invite the tortoise.

5 And the tortoise came anyway, and stood at the edge of the feast, and said:

"You have eaten the yam you cleared. But your mouth is dry and there is no water, for the water was

carried by me."

6 And the goat laughed, and reached for the water pot.

7 And the pot was empty.

8 And the tortoise said:

"I carried the water, and I did not put the whole of it in the ground."

9 And the goat was ashamed before the whole town, and the town said: "The one who digs alone eats alone, and the one who eats alone chokes alone."

Chapter 7 — The Kola That Was Kept

A story of the offering.

1 A poor man came to the Ndose on the day of the festival, and he had nothing.

2 He had no yam, no palm wine, no goat and no cloth. He had one kola nut, and it was the last thing in his house.

3 And he stood at the back, ashamed, while the others brought their offerings forward.

4 And the priest saw him, and called him.

5 And the man said: "I have only this."

6 And the priest took the kola, and cracked it, and laid half of it on the altar, and gave the other half back to the man.

7 And he said:

"The offering is not measured by the field it came from. It is measured by what is left behind. You have

given half of everything you own. Nobody here has given more."

Chapter 8 — The Word That Arrived First

A story of the beginning, and of the errand that was lost.

1 Once Chukwu called the children of wisdom together and told them to choose one from among them who could run, to carry an errand for him into the world.

2 And they went and chose Nkịta, the dog. And Mbe, the tortoise, was angry, and said that it was he who knew more than any of them, and that he was the one fit to carry the errand.

3 And Chukwu said that he had chosen the dog out of all of them. And Chukwu told the dog to go into the world and tell the people that death would not exist in the world — that no one would die, and that every person would remain in the world without end.

4 And the tortoise heard the errand.

5 And he went ahead of the dog and fouled the path, and then he ran on to the world. And the dog, coming along the path, found what the tortoise had left there, and stopped to eat it. And while he was eating, the tortoise had already reached the world, and stood before all the people who had gathered to wait for the word of Chukwu, and said:

"Whether it is done above or done below — death will exist in the world."

6 And the people all broke into weeping.

7 And when the dog arrived at last, he asked them what was the matter, and they told him what the tortoise had said. And the dog told them to kill him, and said that it was he, and not the tortoise, whom Chukwu had sent — and that Chukwu had said that death would not exist in the world.

8 And the people sent to the house of Chukwu to ask which word they should take: the word of the tortoise, or the word of the dog.

9 And Chukwu answered that the word had already gone past him, and had reached the land of the spirits — and that what a people receives first is what it keeps.

10 And that is why death exists in the world to this day.

Chapter 9 — Ewu Chukwu, and the Two Plates

A story of Chukwu's own goat, and of how sickness came into the world.

1 In the town of Iduu there was a man with two wives, and the head wife was very envious of the other.

2 And in that town there was a goat of Chukwu that wandered where it liked. And the people of that town respected that goat, for whoever did a thing to it that brought its cry out of it, Chukwu would not forgive him.

3 One day the child of the second wife saw the goat of Chukwu in their yam plot, eating their yams. And he took up one clod of earth and threw it at the goat, quietly, so that nobody would see.

4 And the goat cried out, and fell down and died.

5 And the head wife and her child raised the alarm and went through the town, saying: "This woman and her child have killed the goat of Chukwu." And the town gathered and drove them out to the edge of the town, saying that they had done alu.

6 And the child thought about what to do, and he went to the house of Chukwu to beg him to forgive him and his mother. And when he got there he told him how it had gone with the goat, and he sang as he went:

Chukwu eze igwe

Chukwu eze igwe

Otu mkpụrụ aja ka m tụrụ ewu Chukwu

Ka ọ na-ata ji m

Ewu Chukwu daa, nwụọ

Kparama

7 And when he had finished the song, Chukwu told him that he would not go home that day, for night had fallen.

8 And Chukwu set two plates before him. On one was meat and fish. On the other was roasted cocoyam. And Chukwu said to him: take the one that is yours, and eat.

9 And the child took the cocoyam and ate it.

10 And when sleep came on him, Chukwu gave him a fine mat spread on a bed, and showed him the place where his goats and his sheep slept. And the child went and slept with the goats and the sheep, on the bare ground where they were.

11 And in the morning Chukwu called him and told him how he would go home. He said that on the road he would hear two sounds. If what he heard was the bleating of the goats, he was to turn aside into the bush and take nothing. But if what he heard was the udu, he was to come out to the path and take it up. And whatever he carried home and broke in his mother's house would show what was inside it.

12 And the child did exactly as Chukwu told him. And when he broke the udu in his mother's house, good things of every kind came out of it — money, and goods, and things beyond counting. And his father and his mother took all of it, and became rich.

13 And it drove the head wife out of her mind.

14 She beat her own son and said to him: "Why did you not kill the goat of Chukwu, so that we too could be rich?" And her son took a stick and beat the goat of Chukwu to death. And his mother told him to run to the house of Chukwu and beg him.

15 And as soon as he came into the house of Chukwu he was looking about him with his eyes for the udu that would make them rich. And before he had told Chukwu how it had gone with him and the goat, Chukwu already knew that he was lying.

16 And Chukwu set the same two plates. And this child took the plate of meat and fish and ate it all.

17 And when he looked about for where he would sleep, Chukwu showed him the fine bed, and showed him also where the goats and the sheep slept. And the child ran and climbed up on the bed.

18 And in the morning Chukwu told him the same thing: the bleating, and the udu; the bush, and the path.

19 And the child ran home, and heard the sound, and thought it was money crying inside the udu, and ran out and carried it home.

20 And when he broke it in his mother's house, there came out of it sickness of every kind — ekpenta, and the pox, and foul diseases without number — and they fastened on him and on his mother. And that is how foul sickness came into the world.

BOOK VIII — The Book of Rites (Isolo Odiana)

(All major ceremonial practices)

Chapter 1 — The Rite of Birth (Ibi Ụmụ)

1 A child is a person from the first breath, and the whole of the religion's care for it begins there. The rite is a welcoming and a naming, and it is not a cleansing — a newborn has done nothing to be cleansed of.

2 Who leads it. The Dibia of the Ndose the family belongs to, with the Ụmụnna standing as witnesses. The mother is present where she is able, and the women of the house stand with her.

3 The time. When the child is healthy and the mother is able — and the cord-rite is done first, for that rite gives the child its standing in the lineage.

4 What is needed. Clean water · nzu, the white chalk · white cloth · kola · and wholesome food to share.

5 The order of the rite.

6 The child is brought to the Dibia, and the Dibia places a hand above the child's head — not on it — and blesses the child to Chi, to Ana and to the Ndi Eri. 7 And he asks for the child health, wisdom, courage, good character, and a long life among its people. 8 Then the names are spoken aloud, before the family and the witnesses: the Aha Chi, the sacred name given in connection with the child's own chi, and then the family name and the personal name. 9 The nzu is marked, and clean water is poured, and the white cloth is laid about the child. 10 And the child's birth is entered in the register of the Ndose — its name, its parentage, and its place in the lineage. 11 Then the family shares kola, and fruit, and wholesome food, and the community eats with them.

12 And the Dibia says:

"Aha gị bụ ndụ gị; ka Chi gị bụrụ ụzọ gị; ka Ana bụrụ ụlọ gị; Chukwu nye gị ume."

Your name is your life; may your Chi be your path; may Ana be your home; God give you strength.

13 And what is not done.

14 No animal is required for this rite, and where the custom of the place asks for one, a fowl is killed and its blood spilled on the ground. The offering is kola, nzu, mmanya and water. 15 Nothing is placed into the child's mouth, and nothing is put into the child's body. 16 The child is not cut, and not marked with a knife, and not held down for any title. A mark a person cannot refuse is not a mark of honour, and this religion puts no owner's sign on a child. 17 No part of the child's body is taken away. The body is not a thing to be corrected. It is a person to be received.

18 And the doctrine of the rite. The child is named before the people, entered in the register, and entrusted to its own destiny. The religion does not own the child. It welcomes it, it names it, and it lets it go to become what it is.

Chapter 2 — The Rite of Marriage (Igba Nkwu)

1 Marriage is the joining of two people, of their families, and of their communities. It is a covenant freely entered by two adults, and it is not the purchase or the transfer of a woman.

2 Who leads it. The couple chooses the Dibia of the Ndose whose authority they wish over their marriage, and he is the principal officiant. The families and the community stand as witnesses — and a marriage of two people with no community around it is not this rite.

3 Who may marry. Two adults, freely, and without coercion of any kind. And the religion does not sell anybody: no woman is bought and no family sells a daughter. Where a gift becomes a price, the marriage is not this rite.

4 The gift, and what it is not. The man and his family bring Ọlụlụ Onyinye — a gift of fellowship: food, cloth, livestock, craft, or another gift according to their means. It has no fixed value. It is not payment for the bride. And it may never be demanded as a condition of the marriage.

5 The choice is made in the open. At the heart of the ceremony the woman takes a cup of palm wine and walks among the gathered people, looking for the man she has chosen. And when she finds him, she offers it to him.

6 Gift honours the union; the wine seals the choice; the Dibia blesses the covenant.

7 And he must drink it. The man receives the cup and drinks from it. He does not pour it away and he does not pass it on — for to accept and to drink is his public word that he accepts her choice and enters the covenant willingly. The wine is not a formality. It is the consent, said in front of everybody.

8 And the consent is asked aloud, of both. The Dibia joins their hands and prays to Chi, to Ana and to the Ndi Eri, and he asks the two of them, before their families and the community, whether they enter it freely. And both answer.

9 And where either does not answer freely, there is no marriage. The Dibia stops the rite, and the community is told why. A covenant made under pressure is not a covenant.

10 And he blesses it:

"Unu abụrụla otu ụzọ; ka ụzọ unu bụrụ nke udo."

You have become one path; may your path be one of peace.

11 And the marriage is entered in the register of the Ndose — the two names, the two lineages, and the day — so that the marriage is known to the religion and not only to the two of them.

12 And what is not done.

13 Nothing is killed for the wedding, and no blood is used. The offering is kola, nzu, mmanya and water. 14 No price is named and no price is paid, and no family is refused because it is poor. 15 No one is married against their will, and no girl is promised before she can refuse. Nothing which matters comes before the choosing.

16 And the doctrine of the rite. The marriage is sealed not by wealth and not by ownership, but by consent, by the blessing of the Dibia, by the witness of the community, and by the shared cup. The gift honours the union; the wine seals the choice; the Dibia blesses the covenant.

Chapter 3 — The Great Rite of Burial (Iru Ana)

1 "Ana bu ndu; onye nwụrụ anwụ alaghachila n'Ana." Ana is life; the one who has died has returned to Ana.

2 Burial is the last rite of the religion and the first duty owed to the dead. The body belongs to Ana and returns to her; the soul goes on to the spirit-land; the lineage keeps the name. These three are one act, and the religion allows none of them to be left undone.

3 The order of the rite is fixed, and it is kept in this order.

4 1. The one who leads, and the ones who answer for it.

5 The Dibia of the dead person's own Ndose leads the rite. He is the only one who may speak the committal. 6 The Ụmụnna — the family and the kindred — carry and bury. They are answerable for the body. 7 The Ndi Nkà, the craftsmen of the lineage, make the Akpati Ana and the lineage artefact. 8 And no one who is not of the Ụmụnna, and not of the Ndose, has any part in it.

9 2. The time.

10 The dead are buried quickly. The body is not kept in the house to be displayed, and it is not held for those who must travel. The religion holds that the ground waits, and that a body kept is a body kept from Ana. The rite is done in the day, and it is not done in the dark.

11 3. The washing of the body.

12 The body — ozu — is washed with clean water. 13 Those who wash it are of the same sex as the dead, and they wash it in silence. 14 Nzu is used in the water, for the body of a person is returned to Ana clean, as it was taken. 15 The body is dried, and it is dressed in akwa ọcha — white cloth, undyed and clean. 16 And the eyes are closed, and the limbs are laid straight.

17 4. What may not be done to the body.

18 No embalming. No chemical is put into the body to hold it. 19 No metal, no plastic, and no cement on the body or about it. 20 The body is not mutilated, and nothing is taken from it but what this rite allows. 21 And nothing is placed in the hand or the mouth of the dead. The dead are not sent with goods. They are sent with their name, which the living keep. 22 No grave is dug before it is needed, and a grave is never reopened.

23 5. Ịchekwa Ebo Ụmụnna — the keeping of the lineage.

24 Before the Akpati Ana is closed, the relic is taken. One izé is removed with respect, and it is prepared for Uneri, the vault. Where the family keeps its own Okpensi, a second izé may be kept for it. The keeping is done once, and it is done for the lineage and not for the household.

25 6. The Akpati Ana.

26 The Akpati Ana is made of woven fibre alone, and of nothing that will not return to the soil. 27 Metal, plastic, cement, chemical treatment and embalming are forbidden in it. 28 It is a vessel and not a monument. The body is being returned, and the vessel is returning with it. 29 Flowers may be laid on it or about it as an honour and a remembrance. They carry no rite and are owed to no one.

30 7. The blessing of return.

31 The Dibia stands beside the Akpati before it is carried out, and he blesses the body to Chi, to Ana and to the Ndi Eri.

"Ihe Ana nyere, Ana na-anata. Ka ozu laghachi n'Ana, ka Chi gị gaa n'ụzọ ya."

What Ana gives, Ana receives. May the body return to Ana, and may your Chi continue upon its path.

32 And the family says farewell, and the Akpati is lifted.

33 8. The way to the grave.

34 The Akpati is carried to the ground by the Ụmụnna, and the party goes in silence. The way is not lined, and no one is hired to weep. The dead are accompanied by the people who owe them the carrying, and by nobody who is paid.

35 9. The grave.

36 Burial is always in the ground. There is no other disposal in this religion. 37 The grave faces east, towards Anyanwu Ututu, and the head is laid to the east. 38 The grave is dug with hand tools, and it is left rough on the inside, for it is Ana's and not a work of joinery. 39 Where the ground is wet, the grave is sited or drained so that the Akpati never stands in water. The Akpati is never laid in standing water, in dry land, in wetland or in mangrove ground. 40 The body is laid on its right side, facing east, and earth is returned to earth over it. 41 The grave is filled by the Ụmụnna, by hand. And it is not opened again — not for a relic, not for a second body, and not for anything.

42 10. Iru Ana — the seven clods.

43 The elder appointed by the Ụmụnna stands at the head of the grave and casts seven clods of earth into it. One clod for each of the seven — the four corners of the compound, and the three paths that leave the town. And he names the ancestors of the lineage as he casts them.

44 Then the name of the dead is spoken aloud, and it is entered in the register of the Ndose, and in the Mkpuru-Ndụ of the lineage.

45 And the elder says:

"Ọ laghachila n'Ana. Aha ya dị ndụ."

He has returned to Ana. His name is alive.

46 11. The mourning, and the cleansing of the house.

47 The household keeps its own ground clean in the days of the death. 48 The bereaved do not enter the Ndose until the Dibia has set the cleansing and it is done. 49 A widow or a widower keeps the mourning the lineage sets, and it is not longer than the lineage says. 50 And the burial of a head is kept with an animal — a goat where the house can, and a fowl where it cannot — and its blood is spilled on the ground at the grave, and the meat is eaten by those who dug it. And the ordinary burial of a household is kept with kola, nzu, mmanya and water, and no animal is required of it.

51 12. The burial ground stays a living place.

52 Small plants and herbs may be set above or beside the grave, and the family is encouraged to set them. They are living memorials, and they keep the burial ground part of the landscape of the living rather than a place cut off from it. But no wall is raised to shut the dead away, and no grave is made a monument.

53 13. The continuity of the lineage.

54 The izé kept for Uneri is taken to the vault, and the izé kept for the family goes to the Okpensi. The Ndi Nkà work them into the lineage artefact, and the artefact is kept by the lineage and not by a household. Where the family has an Okpensi, a relic may be set there also. And the grave is not disturbed to make any of it.

55 14. The doctrine of the rite, in one paragraph.

56 The body returns to Ana, and Ana remembers it. The soul goes to the spirit-land and is judged there. The lineage keeps the name. So the dead are not erased, and they are not turned into gods. They return to Ana, they enter the memory of the people, and they continue through the Ndi Eri and the generations after them — which is why the religion buries its dead rather than keeping them, and why it keeps the name rather than the body.

Chapter 4 — Ọmalinze, the Child the Water Kept

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 There was a king who had many wives, and not one of them bore him a son. He loved two of them, and he hated one, and the hatred was not for anything the woman had done.

2 And in his compound there was a place where the aja was made, and the wife he hated was kept there, at the back, out of sight.

3 And the king went to Arọchukwu to ask why he had no male child. And Chukwu told him the reason: his own father had wasted the goods of the poor and taken all their land. And he told him that if he greatly wanted a son, he must first give back to the children of the poor every plot his father had gathered from them.

4 And the king did it.

5 Then the dibia he had brought home from Arọchukwu divined for him again, and told him the other thing he must do: he must go and pluck one bunch of the akwụ, and string the seeds for all his wives, and let each wife chew her string. And one seed among them carried the promise — whichever wife chewed that one would bear him the son he was asking for. And the dibia charged him that no woman who was not his wife was to chew it.

6 And the king strung the seeds with his own hand, and gave a string to every wife except the one he hated, and warned the others not to give her any of theirs. For he said it would be alu if the wife he hated bore him a firstborn son.

7 Now the head wife took her string into her room, and found in it one seed that stood out hard and dark from the rest. She threw it out into the yard, saying it was of no use to her.

8 And a lizard on the wall took it and carried it to the wife who lived at the place of the aja.

9 And that woman chewed it.

10 And in time every wife was with child, and it was found that she was with child also, and the others laughed at her and said there was a stone in her womb.

11 And before the day came, the king gave his servant a law: that any female child born should be thrown into the water, and only the males brought home.

12 And in the night the wives went down to the waterside to be delivered, and one after another they bore daughters, and the servant threw them into the water, as the law said. And last, in secret, the hated wife came and bore a son, and he was shining.

13 And when the king's servant saw him, grief took him, and he threw the two of them in — and she had no strength left in her to save herself and her child, and the water carried them away.

14 And the water carried them to a place where an old woman was washing at the river's edge. Pity took her; she gathered them up and carried them home. And she nursed them until the woman was well again, and then the woman went back to the compound, to the place of the aja, and the old woman kept the boy.

15 And he grew, and he was very handsome and very strong, and the old woman named him Ọmalinze.

16 And every night the old woman went to market and bought him food. But in the middle of the day, when she was gone, the king's dog — the dog that had been at the waterside on the night he was thrown — came to him and licked him.

17 And whenever the dog came, the child sang:

Nna m eze nyere iwu

Ọ mụrụ nwoke, kpọlata

Ọ mụrụ nwaanyị, tụfuo

Odibo eze, onye iwu

E wee mụta m, tụfuo

Odibo eze, onye iwu

Nnyaa, Nnyaako!

18 And he sang it and did not know that a child of a dibia was up a palm tree tapping wine, and heard every word of it.

19 And that child came to the king one evening and told him what he heard in the middle of every day. And the king went with him, and heard it with his own ears.

20 Then the king seized his servant and put him in chains, and he brought the old woman to his house and thanked her and gave her many gifts. And he asked her to tell him the woman who had borne the boy.

21 And the old woman said:

"One truth I will give you: the boy is your own son. But I will not tell you the woman who bore him, for if I told you, you would not believe me. That is a thing you will find out for yourself."

22 And the king's other wives began to say that the boy was theirs, each of them. So a day was fixed, and on that day the boy was to come and eat from the hand of the woman who had borne him.

23 And on that day the other wives pounded yam and cooked rich soup and dressed themselves, and came early. And the woman at the place of the aja was still cooking.

24 And as Ọmalinze came into the king's compound, one of the flute players who had come with the dancers took him with his ọja and played:

Ọmalinze, Ọmalinze, Okoro ọma

Ọmalinze, na nne gị nọ n'ọtụtụ aja

Ọmalinze, Ọmalinze, Okoro ọma

Nwa nze, nwa nze, nwa nze, Okoro ọma

25 And the boy would not eat from any of the women who came forward. He went to the place where the aja was made, and ate there — and the flute played it again as he went — and the woman who was hated, and who was his mother, fed him before he had finished.

26 And the whole assembly knew.

27 Then the king gave the law that she be brought out of the place where she had been kept. And she was given soap, and she washed her body well, and fine cloth was found for her to wear. And the king took her and his son up into his upper house.

28 And from that day it was she who said what was done in the compound and in the house of the king, and the others followed her.

Chapter 5 — Okoro Udo, and the Leopard Who Came to Marry

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 There was a man who was a carver, and his name was Okoro Udo. He carved the stools and the seats and the things a house needs, and what he carved was so fine that it was as if a spirit had carved it, and people came from far places to him.

2 And when his wood was finished he went into the forest to cut more. And he walked a long way and found no good wood, and went deeper, and at last he saw one great tree whose branches were what he wanted.

3 And he climbed it, and cut.

4 And he did not know that a leopard had left her cubs at the foot of that tree, and had gone to find them food.

5 And when the branch came down, it fell on the cubs and killed them. And the man did not know. And he carried his wood home.

6 And the leopard came back and found them, and buried them, and she swore an oath that she would be the death of the man who had done it.

7 And when she had buried them she waited for night, and then she took off her leopard's skin and became a beautiful young woman. And she put a vessel of ufie on her head, and went into the town selling camwood.

8 And the young men of the town came running to see her. And she said: "I will marry the man who can throw one kernel into the mouth of my ufie pot."

9 And they came, each of them, and threw three times, and failed, and called the next one. And every young man in that town was tired out — but she was watching all the while for the one she had come for.

10 And then they remembered Okoro Udo, who had not come. And they went to his house and called him, and he said he did not want to waste his time, for he was no better than those who had failed. And they would not leave him alone, and he got up and said he would try.

11 And he threw, and the kernel went into the pot.

12 And the town shouted, and he took her home. And when they came into his compound, the dog he had began to growl at her.

13 And he called the puppy and told it that the woman was now its mistress. And the puppy looked at her a long time, and said nothing, and went and lay down by the fire.

14 But its eyes were on her wherever she was.

15 And that night the man and his wife lay down to sleep, and the dog lay down in the room where they slept, as it had always done. And in the middle of the night the woman saw that the man was asleep, and got up and put on her leopard's skin, and was coming to take his throat.

16 And the dog barked.

17 And the man woke, and the woman was a woman again, and she complained that the dog would not let her sleep. And the man scolded the dog. And the dog was not a person. It could not tell its master what it had seen. So it lay down and was quiet.

18 And it happened a second time, and the dog bit her, and the man scolded it again. And the woman knew that she could not do it in the house.

19 And she asked him to keep the dog outside. And he did, because he did not know whether madness was beginning in it.

20 And that night the woman got up, and the puppy put its head down at the door and barked and threw itself about, and the man woke again.

21 And the man grew angry with the dog, and got up and went outside and sat there until dawn, and then he swept the compound.

22 And afterwards his wood was finished, and he told his wife that he was going into the forest to cut more, and she said she would come with him and gather firewood.

23 And whenever they saw firewood she said it was no good, and that they should look for wood that burns bright. And she led him, and led him, until they came to the foot of the tree he had cut that first time.

24 And she lay down there. And she asked him to climb up and gather firewood for her. And he climbed.

25 And when he called her to come out, and the wood was ready to fall, he called her, and he called her three times, and there was no answer. And he looked down to see why she had not answered him.

26 And he saw a leopard.

27 And he shouted that a leopard had eaten his wife. And the leopard answered him, and said that she was his wife — that he had killed her children with firewood, and that she had made herself a woman and come to marry him and be the answer to it, but that his dog would not let her; and that now she had him where his dog was not.

28 And he begged her, and said that he had not known. And he begged her to forgive him. And she refused, and said that what she had said would be done.

29 And the man had a horn of medicine in a niche in the wall of his house. And while he was up in that tree the horn began to sound by itself, and to call the people, and this is what it called:

Okoro Udo ee-ee — Okoro Udo

Okoro Udo ee-ee — Okoro Udo

30 and it said that the one he lived with was a leopard, and that Okoro Udo was being killed in the forest.

31 And the people heard the horn sounding by itself, and they gathered and listened to what it said, and it troubled them, and they did not know where to look for him. And they brought the dog and hung the horn on its neck, and told it to lead them with its nose to where its master was.

32 And the dog ran off at once. And the people followed it with guns and knives, and the horn sounded as they ran.

33 And the man up in the tree heard that it was the horn, and hope came into him that help was on the road. And he begged her again — as a leopard — to forgive him and go her own way while there was still time. And she refused.

34 And while she stood waiting for him to come down, the people came. And as soon as she saw them she sprang, and charged.

35 And the dog did not wait for her. It went at her, leopard against leopard, and the two of them fought — and the fight gave the people the ground to come close, and they shot her and cut her, and she died.

36 And the man came down out of the tree.

37 And he was not glad that she was dead. He told himself that it was a thing he had brought upon himself. And he thanked the household, and went home with them.

38 And from that day he kept his eye on his dog and on his horn, and took care of them; for with the two of them gone he would have gone and looked at a dead man.

Chapter 6 — The Slave at the Second Burial

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 A father was going on a journey, and before he went he set his house in order.

2 He left two of his own — Ugo and Aghumme. He left a cock with a flaming crest. And he left a ram for the Abia rites, the dance the men dance for the dead.

3 And he said:

"Should I return from my travel, I shall take Ugo and Aghumme, and I shall take this cock with the flaming crest, and this ram for the Abia rites, and I shall do honour to my father.

But should I get lost in my travel — make use of Ugo and Aghumme. Kill this cock with the flaming crest. Kill this ram for the Abia rites — for my second burial."

4 And the father did not come back.

5 And his slave tied the son to the stake.

6 And he sounded the talking gongs all round the town, and called the kindred and the elders:

"Let every house bring out the staff of its fathers. Let every holder of the ofo bring the ofo. For the father's second burial!"

7 The gongs were heard in the compounds, and the people came out. And the man they had come to bury was tied to a stake in his own father's compound.

8 And the son spoke to them from the stake.

9 He asked the question the tale is remembered for:

"Now, a question to you, our elders: should a true son be used for his father's rites?

In the good old days, I have learned, a slave was used for his master's burial!"

10 And the spell was broken, and the truth came out.

11 The slave was used for his master's rites.

Chapter 7 — The Bride the Water Kept

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 It was a day for rejoicing, but not an entirely happy one.

"What can we do, my sister — we do not marry our daughters here!"

2 Mgbafo-Ocha was going far away, to the house of the man she would marry. She had many things to take with her, and she would not go alone: a maid, and her little sister, went with her.

3 At dusk a great crowd of young girls saw the three of them off for the first part of the way. The place was far, and they walked fast to be out of the midday blaze. And they were crossing a stream close by the journey's end when the maid pushed her mistress into the swiftly running water.

4 The little sister ran wildly, and was overpowered.

5 Mgbafo was drowned — but the water kept her.

6 And the maid went on to the house, and lived there as the wife, and the little girl was made to serve her.

7 Day after day the girl carried a water pot down to the stream — a pot far too big for her, for she must obey her mistress — and day after day she wept for her sister, and sang:

"My sister, Mgbafo-Ocha —

the corpse, rock-heavy thing,

the corpse that knows not its husband!

My sister, Mgbafo-Ocha —

they are eating yams: your sister is starving.

They are eating coco yams: your sister is starving.

They are eating meat: your sister is starving.

They are eating fish: your sister is starving."

8 And there was a sudden splash, and Mgbafo stood in the water, as dazzling as a mirror.

9 Her sister ran to hold her, and could not. For all that she was there, she was out of reach of living people.

10 But she helped her sister with the heavy pot, and she stood and looked on until the girl had climbed the steep rise and was gone.

11 And rumours of the appearances began to spread in that place. And the little girl carried one thought that she could not put down: the fishes were slowly eating her sister.

12 She told her fear to a close friend, and the story reached her master.

13 So she went down to the riverside with her pot, and cried in her usual manner. It was morning. The stream parted with a splash, and the beauty appeared. And while Mgbafo stood by her sister, the man who had been hiding closed in on her.

14 She tried to escape. There was a bitter struggle, and the whole ground was covered with breadfruit slime, and in the end Mgbafo was mastered.

15 Her sister was overjoyed.

16 And the wicked maid who had become a wife was sent away in disgrace.

17 And the young man knew his wife again, and knew what had been done to her.

Chapter 8 — Ichu Aja, the Driving Away

1 Ichu Aja is the clearing away of what interferes. And the name carries its own meaning: aja is the loose earth — the sand, the dust, the thing that settles upon a thing and cloaks it — and to chu aja is to drive it off. The religion keeps the name and gives it back its own sense: not a killing, but a driving away.

2 And the second sense of the name is kept also: aja is a field of a life, the portion handed down that sustains a person. So Ichu Aja is at once the driving off of what spoils, and the going after of what sustains.

3 And the purpose of it is single. It is to take away what stands between a person and the proper flow of his own life — the blockage, and the stagnation, and the thing left over from what went wrong.

4 And what the religion counts as aja: the grudge kept · the debt unpaid · the lie left standing · the wrong done and never owned · the ground left fouled · and the habit that has come to master the person who keeps it.

5 And the religion says this plainly: aja is not always a substance that can be washed off from outside. Some of it is only in the person. No altar clears what a man will not put down.

6 And the first shrine of Ichu Aja is the body. Before any person keeps an altar, he keeps the one given him — and the religion takes that literally, and not as a figure of speech.

7 And the body is already built to clear itself. The heart drives the blood through it and does not rest; the lungs take in what feeds and put out what is spent; the liver strains; the kidneys wash; the gut keeps what nourishes and lets go of what does not; the skin closes; and the bone knits. Nobody taught it any of this, and no one keeps it running. It was made this way. So the first instrument of purification in Odiana is not the shrine. It is the person.

8 And therefore the religion does not despise the body, and does not punish it, and does not call it filthy. A shrine is kept clean because it is a shrine, and not because it is dirt.

9 And the highest of the means is the fast — Ibu Onu — which has its own chapter after this one.

10 And the other means, in the order the religion keeps them.
