11 First, the putting down of the thing itself — the debt paid, the apology made, the grudge released, and the wrong owned aloud. This comes before every rite, for it is the only part of the clearing that nobody else can do for you.

12 Second, the ground — the compound swept and cleared to its edges, the drains opened, the paths kept, and nothing left rotting where people live. A person does not clear himself while standing in filth, and the religion does not accept a clean altar in a dirty place.

13 Third, the washing — the body washed, and the hands washed at the water, and nzu, the white chalk, marked. And at the washing the person says what he is putting down, and does not say it as a formula.

14 Fourth, the fast — for the fast is the clearing that goes on where nobody can see it, and it is therefore the deepest.

15 Fifth, the offering — the first fruits laid down whole, and an animal killed where the clearing is grave. And the offering is brought after the clearing, and not instead of it.

16 And what Ichu Aja is not. It is not the buying off of a wrong. A wrong that a person can set right must be set right by that person. An offering does not stand in the place of the thing you owe. And a wrong that only the law can answer is answered at the law.

17 Ikpu Alu is the cleansing of an abomination, and the animal is set by the weight of the thing. A minor abomination is cleared with fowl; a great one with a live he-goat and sixteen yams; and some of the gravest with a cow — as the ancestors set it down, and it is kept. And the animal carries the abomination away, as the fowl carries a sickness to the wilderness and is left there. This is why the animal is not a payment: it is a bearer.

18 And the blood is spilled on open ground, away from the shrine, and it is not brought to the altar at all. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water — and the ground takes the blood, for the ground is what was wronged.

19 And the religion gives one warning, and gives it to everybody. Do not chase the clearing of the outside while the inside stands untouched. To do the rite and keep the habit is not purification; it is performance — and the person who does it will feel relieved, and will be unchanged. Some seek every clearing but the one within them, and take relief that does not last, and are afterwards more confused than they were.

20 And the one who has truly cleared says nothing about it. He is not seen fasting, and his washing is not announced, and he does not tell the town what he has put down. What has been driven off does not need a witness.

Chapter 9 — Ibu Onu, the Fast

1 Ibu Onu is the fast. And the religion holds it to be the highest form of Ichu Aja. Not because it is hard, but because it works upon the one shrine that every person carries and that no person can hand over to another.

2 And what a fast is in Odiana. A person sets aside, for a fixed number of days, from one thing to four things — and he names them aloud before he begins, so that the fast has an edge to it and not merely a feeling.

3 And the thing set aside need not be food. A person may as rightly fast from the palm wine, from the quarrel, from the market, from the talk that spoils a name, or from the screen at night. But the chief fast, and the one the religion means when it says Ibu Onu and no more, is the fast from food.

4 And the fast is Ete Ululu — the bridge set in front and the body behind it — as it is set out in the Book of Afa. So a fast is not the punishment of the body. It is the reordering of what leads.

5 And the person names his intention with the fast — cleansing, or renewal, or growth, or healing, or preparation for what is coming, or gratitude — and the abstention is the reminder of it, carried in the body all day where it cannot be forgotten.

6 And the fasts of the religion as a whole are three.

7 The Ọnwa Ụbi — the fast of the ground in the month before the Ubi — which is not a fast of meat but of new things, and which is set out in the Book of Festivals. That is the fast of the whole land, and it is kept by the land and not by choice.

8 And the fast of the year, Ibu Onu Afọ — kept before Igu Aro, for the number of days the council names, in which the people put the year's quarrels and debts in order and come to the speaking of the year with clean hands. What is fasted from is set by the council, and no household is bound past what it can carry.

9 And the personal fast — kept by any person at any need: before a great undertaking, in a sickness, before a reading, at a death in the house, or when a person cannot say what is wrong with him and knows only that something is. And for this no permission is needed from anybody.

10 And the lengths. A fast may be a day, or a fixed number of days, or a season. And the religion sets no merit upon length, and forbids any fast past what the body can carry without harm. Sickness ends a fast, and the ending of it is not a failure. Whoever breaks a fast because his body failed him has kept the whole of the law; whoever presses on and damages himself has broken it.

11 And water is not refused in a fast of Odiana. This is not a religion of the dried throat.

12 And the weak are not bound. The sick, the aged, the nursing mother, the child, and the one whose work would injure him are carried by the fast of others and do not keep it. And the fast is kept by the strong for the sake of the whole, and the weak are carried by it. And a Ndose that shames such a person has broken the fast itself.

13 And the doing of it: the person rises before the sun and washes; he says what he is putting down; he keeps the day's work and does not lie about in idleness; he speaks little and does not pick quarrels; and he comes to the evening and reads himself. And if a man fasts and comes out of it angrier, or sharper of tongue, or prouder than he was in the morning, then what he put down has not gone anywhere.

14 And the breaking of the fast is a feast and not a relief. The fast is ended with food, and the food is shared, and a portion of it goes to a household that could not keep the fast. The fast ends in Isalaka, and a fast that ends alone has ended in nothing.

15 And the religion forbids four fasts.

16 A fast kept to be seen — and the one who announces his fast has been paid for it, and must not expect to be paid a second time.

17 A fast kept as a bargain — as though food were a price, and the fast a payment that obliges anybody to do anything.

18 A fast kept as a punishment of the body, in the belief that the body is the enemy of the person who has it. The religion does not hold that. A person who hates his own body has not understood the shrine he was given.

19 And a fast kept as an offering for a wrong — for a wrong is answered by putting it right, and not by going without. And the religion says it a second time, since it is the first thing people forget: an offering does not stand in the place of the thing you owe.

20 And no fast makes a person greater than his neighbour, and the one who has fasted longest is not the holiest man in the Ndose. The fast is a private clearing, and it is not a rank.

21 And the religion's word upon it is this: the person who has fasted has learned something about himself that nobody could have told him. And what he learned, he keeps.

Chapter 10 — Obara, the Blood

1 Obara is blood, and blood is life. It is a liquid form of life, as water is a liquid form of life, and it carries the living force within it.

2 And the religion teaches what blood is made of, and why it does what it does. The thin part of it — the liquid — answers to mmuo, the spirit, and to the unseen life. And the thick part of it answers to mmadu, the human being, and to the body. So blood is the one substance in a person or an animal that holds both at once, and that is why it joins the two worlds when nothing else will.

3 And blood is used for three things in this religion, and no more.

4 And in this religion the blood is not put upon the shrine, and not upon the Ofo, and not upon the Ikenga, and not upon a medicine or any sacred thing. The old practice gave such things a life of their own by blood. Odiana does not. A shrine is set apart with kola, and nzu, and wine, and water, and with the words said over it — and it is kept immaculate, as a swept floor is kept.

5 To feed the ancestors and the spirits. In the days when a household killed its own meat, the blood was caught as the animal died and was not thrown away. It was poured out for the family's own dead and for the spirits of the place — upon the ground, and away from the shrine and from any sacred thing — and it was poured with words and not in silence.

6 And to honour the land. The ground is fed, for the ground feeds the town.

7 And the manner of the killing is the whole of the law, and a person who gets this wrong has done nothing. It is not violence. It is a duty. It is done slowly of the will and quickly of the hand, with intention, and with the least pain the thing can be given — and among the old lineages the animal was spoken to before it was killed, because it was known what was being done and to whom. An animal tormented has been taken badly, and a bad taking is not an offering.

8 And no part of the animal is wasted. The blood is given, and the meat is eaten, and the hide and the horn and the bone are used. The living eat what the dead were given the blood of, and the two eat together.

9 And the religion tells the truth about where the blood goes, since it is asked. In the old practice the blood was poured upon the altars, and upon the sacred trees, and upon the earth. In Odiana the blood is not brought to the shrine at all, and not to the altar, and not to a tree that is held sacred. It is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing, and the shrine keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana, and the religion says so in law and not in whispers — the old way was not wrong in its own place and time: it belonged to a household that killed its own meat at its own door. Odiana is not that, and does not pretend to be.

10 And the religion teaches the old rule of the hand that kills. The shedding of blood is not laid on a woman who has not yet passed her change, for she is held to be already close to the mysteries of life and of death through her own blood and through childbearing. So the killing falls to the men, and a woman calls a man to it, and this is not a lesser part: she who does not kill is not thereby outside the rite.

11 And the religion says plainly what this rule is and is not. It is the old custom, kept — and it is a rule about the hand and not about standing. A woman may hold every order of Dibia in this religion, and read, and cleanse, and consecrate, and speak the words over the animal. She does not take the knife. Whether the religion should keep this at all is a question the council must settle and not the scribe.

12 And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. The shedding of human blood upon the earth is the thing that made the earth sacred in the first place, and it is the abomination that has no cleansing. Where the old practice used a human being, or a slave, or a child, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that carries the trouble away, and it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.

Chapter 11 — Nnabata Odiana, the Becoming an Odianian

1 Becoming an Odianian is not being born in a place, and not being of a family, and not speaking a tongue. It is a profession made in the open, and a rite kept once, and a way of walking kept afterwards.

2 And the one thing required of a person at the door is belief in Ana, the mother earth. Nothing else is asked of him. He must believe that the ground is alive, and that she remembers, and that through her the heart of Chukwu is reached.

3 And a person may come from any house, and any town, and any faith he was raised in. He is not asked to curse the house he came from — for a person does not arrive at the ground by despising the road he walked to get to it. He is asked only to say what he now believes, and then to walk on it.

4 And the rite is kept in the open, on bare ground, and not on a floor and not on a mat. The person stands on her herself, with nothing between his feet and the earth.

5 Who keeps it. A Dibia of the Ndose the person is entering, with the Ụmụnna and the households standing as witnesses.

6 What is needed. Clean water · nzu, the white chalk · a kola nut · a bowl of palm wine · and an animal where the house can bring one.

7 And the animal, where it is brought, is a fowl at the least and a goat where the household is able — and it is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground and away from the shrine, as at every killing of this religion. And the meat is cooked and eaten by everybody who came, and no one who came is left out of the eating.

8 And the order of the rite.

9 The person takes off his shoes and stands on the bare ground. And the Dibia says: "Gu zo na ya. Ị naghị zo na ihe." — Stand on her. You are not standing on a thing.

10 And the person takes up a handful of the earth and holds it. He is not asked to kiss it, and not asked to lift it up. He is asked to hold it in his hand while he says what he believes — for this profession is made with the earth in the hand, and not with the hand upon the heart.

11 And the Dibia asks him three questions, and he answers every one of them aloud.

12 "Do you believe that the ground is alive?"

13 "Do you believe that she remembers what is done upon her?"

14 "Do you believe that through her the heart of Chukwu is reached?"

15 And the person answers each one, and the answer is his own, and it is spoken in his own words and is not repeated after anybody.

16 Then he speaks the profession:

"Ekwenyere m na Ana. Ọ bụ ana dị ndụ, ọ na-echeta, ọ bụ ya bụ ụzọ. Site na ya ka e si eru obi Chukwu."

I believe in Ana. She is the living ground, she remembers, and she is the way. Through her the heart of Chukwu is reached.

17 And the Dibia marks him with nzu — on the forehead, and on the back of each hand — and pours clean water upon the ground at his feet, and the earth he is holding he lets fall back upon the earth.

18 And then the kola is broken, and the wine is poured, and the animal is killed where one was brought, and the whole company eats.

19 And the person's name is entered in the register of the Ndose — his name, and the house he came from, and the day he came. And the register says not what he was, but what he professed.

20 And the name. He keeps the name he came with, for a person is not made new by a new word. And where he chooses, he takes a name of his own beside it, and it is written beside the other.

21 And of children. A child born to an Odianian is brought up in it, and makes the profession himself when he is grown enough to answer for it — and until that day he is carried by the household, as the weak are carried by the fast.

22 And of leaving. A person may leave, and may say so plainly, and no one is shamed for it and no one is pursued. And the religion says what the old teachers said: what is walked away from is not thereby erased. The ground is still under him, and she will remember him, and the religion does not pretend otherwise.

23 And no one is an Odianian because his father was one, or because he was born in the town, or because he is not something else. A person is an Odianian because he believes in Ana and walks on her as a child walks on his mother's ground.

BOOK IX — The Book of Light (Iwu Uchu)

(Initiation, enlightenment, pathfinding)

Initiation, cleansing, and the path.

Chapter 1 — What the light is

1 The light is not a flame. It is order, and truth, and the capacity to be understood. 2 Where the light is present, confusion gives way to pattern. Where it is resisted, disorder follows. 3 Anyanwu is its witness and not its source. The source is Chukwu, and Anyanwu only carries the news of it across the sky.

Chapter 2 — Iwu Uchu — the Cleansing

1 A person or a place that has been defiled is cleansed by a licensed priest, and by no one else. 2 The materials are these, and only these: clean water · nzu, the white chalk · white cloth · the leaf of ogilisi · the leaf of uziza · salt · and fire. 3 The cleansing is done in seven steps: 4 First, the ground is cleared and the boundary is re-marked with nzu. 5 Second, clean water is poured — at the threshold and at the altar. 6 Third, the surfaces are washed with water in which nzu has been dissolved. 7 Fourth, ogilisi or uziza is burned, and the smoke is carried through the space. 8 Fifth, white cloth is laid or hung. 9 Sixth, the priest makes the declaration, and those present answer. 10 Seventh, the water is taken away and poured where it will foul nothing. 11 Nothing is killed in any part of this, and nothing used pollutes land or water.

Chapter 3 — The three methods of Iwu Uchu

1 The cleansing is done by one of three methods, and which one is used depends on the kind of uchu the person is carrying. 2 The bath of herbs. A concoction is made from roots and leaves, and the person bathes in it. This is the method for the uchu that has settled into the body. 3 The bath at flowing water. The person is washed at a running stream and not at a standing pool — for the tradition holds that water which moves carries away, and water which stands keeps. The people do not go into the water; the washing is done at its edge, and nothing that is used pollutes the water or the land. 4 The soap. The same herbs are turned into a soap, Ncha Iwu Uchu, and the person washes with it at home, keeping the discipline over a period of days and not in a single hour. 5 And the strongest of the cleansings is made with ose oji, okpote and sea salt — the salt being the strongest of the three — and it is used where the uchu is old and has not answered the gentler means. 6 No method kills anything, and no method uses blood.

Chapter 4 — The kinds of uchu, and where they come from

1 Uchu is not one thing. The tradition names them — Uchu, Orakwu, Uke, Akalogheli, Ogbonuke — the states that disturb a person's alignment. And where they are left, Nseke follows, which is misfortune and destruction. 2 And some uchu are made by the person's own hand. Sexual indiscipline. Wickedness and injustice — Imegbu mmadu. And drunkenness and gluttony, which is the indiscipline of the mouth, and which leads a person to eat what his chi and his Ezumezu abhor. 3 And some uchu are not. The tradition calls it mmụọ igba mmadụ uchu — a spirit riding a person with uchu. It comes from a spirit that was offended, or from a spirit acting as the instrument of another's complaint — and it is the hardest kind to find and the hardest to settle. 4 And this is why the cleansing is not a punishment. The tradition says plainly what the uchu is for: it is a tool the spirits use to get a response out of a person who will not turn, and the response they want is a change of behaviour. 5 And where the source is a spirit, the cleansing exists to bring about reconciliation and restitution and to strike the balance, so that whoever was offended is answered and peace is restored. 6 So Iwu Uchu is never only a washing. It is a washing and the settling of what caused it, and the priest who washes without the settling has done half the work. 7 And the three kinds of nso are named: nso ana, the taboos of the ground; nso chi, the taboos of a person's own chi; and nso ndi ichie, the taboos of the ancestors. The cleansing is done for whichever of the three was broken — for example, at Idemili a person may not eat eke, the python, and to eat it is to break nso ana and to require Iwu Uchu. 8 And a person keeps coming. The tradition does not make Iwu Uchu one remedy for one fault: whatever a person does often, he comes to be cleansed for often. It is a practice and not an event. 9 And the reason the religion asks for it continually is the osenabu — the inner eye, which the tradition also calls the third eye. Uchu clouds it, and the cleansing keeps it clear, so that a person can see the road he is actually on.

Chapter 5 — The greater cleansing

1 When the defilement is alu — an abomination — the cleansing is the same seven steps, and three things are added. 2 The community is present, for the wrong was done to the whole community and not to one person. 3 Restitution is made where a person was harmed, as the law requires. 4 And a period of keeping follows, in which the person or the place observes the daily discipline of cleanliness without a single exception. 5 There is no killing in it. Where the old law demanded an animal, Odiana pours water, applies nzu, burns the leaf, and keeps clean — and this is the law of Odiana.

Chapter 6 — The path

1 The initiate is taught the law, the purity code, the calendar and the tradition. 2 He learns that the light is kept and not seized — that it grows in a person who sweeps, who washes, who speaks the truth and who keeps his word. 3 And he is sent out to keep it.

Chapter 7 — The Mysterious Messengers

A story of Ézè Ǹrì, and of why there are four markets.

1 In the early years of the kingdom, the Ikala was faced with a crisis — and the crisis was that the people were too successful.

2 His advisers came to him with it, and he received them in his obi, and he sat in the central seat at the top of the long hall while the elders took the seats in rows along either side.

3 And he broke the kola.

4 And the head said: "You say the people are too successful?"

5 And one of them said: "It is not a problem in itself. Our people are strong. Our harvests are plenty, and our homes keep multiplying."

6 And another said: "The problem is not our people at all. But the people are hardworking, and everybody is competing to sell everything they have grown or created. It is not smooth."

7 And the head said: "I understand better. What do you propose?" For he had an idea, and he wished to hear theirs first.

8 And the council said: "We do not know. This affects all our families, so we believe the answer should come from you."

9 And the head said: "I will go and ask for an answer, and then I will let you know."

10 And Chukwu sent him strangers.

11 Four of them came, and each carried a basket. They would not disclose their names. And the head received them, and fed them, and said nothing.

12 But in the night he sent rats into their baskets — and the rats turned the things in the baskets, and the baskets named the men.

13 And in the morning the head called them by name:

14 Eke! Oye! Afo! Nkwo!

15 And the people praised his wisdom. And the four spoke, and said:

"Have four markets and four days. Call them Eke, Oye, Afo, Nkwo."

16 And they vanished.

17 And from that day the markets were held in turn, and one town's market did not fall on the day of another's — and the selling was smooth, and the quarrelling over the trade stopped, and the week itself was given to the people as the answer to a problem of business.

BOOK X — The Book of the Priesthood (Uka Odiana)

(Priestly office, consecration, authority)

The office, the orders, the vestments, and the ordination.

Chapter 1 — The orders of the religion

1 Ikala — the head of Odiana. His authority is absolute, and it is not shared. He does not sacrifice and he does not officiate; he appoints the one who does. His work is to authorise, to license, to judge and to cleanse.

2 And there is no second-in-command. This is deliberate. The head holds the abrogation of taboo alone, and a religion that invents a deputy invents a rival. So no office in Odiana outranks another, and none of them sits in his seat.

3 Three offices stand beneath him, and two bodies.

4 Idenze — the head of the state council. He speaks with the head's voice. He carries the Ikala's word, oversees the works of the religion and its dealings abroad, and answers for its fabric and its goods. He holds no rank above any other, and his office ends the moment the Ikala dies. He is the head's hand, and a hand is not a successor.

5 Alo — the custody of the house, and it is held by the Iyi. While the Ikala lives she holds the sacred things: the reserve ofo, the register, the seal, and the vault Uneri. And the moment the Ikala dies she becomes the administrator of the whole religion until a successor is confirmed. She is the only person in Odiana whose authority grows at the head's death.

6 Ndi Ikenye — the heads of the works, and they are the leaders of the men who hold no title. Each great work has a head, and each answers to the Ikala alone: the law · the purity code · the calendar and the festivals · the priesthood and its licensing · the schools · the healing houses · the vault · and afa.

7 And beneath the council, the Ndi Nze — the titled men — and the age-grades, headed by their isi ogbo, who execute what the council decides.

8 And the two bodies: Nzemabua, the council of state, which advises and cannot command; and the college of Eze Ana, every diocesan head together, which elects the next Ikala and confirms him. The seat belongs to a body, and not to a man.

9 Iyi — the female head. She is not the Ikala's equal, and she is the most powerful person in the religion after him. She holds the women's order, the rites of fertility, and the purity of marriage and of childbirth; the school and the healing house are hers; she holds a seat in the council in her own right; and she does not bow or kneel before any human being — not before the Ikala, and not before the college. Her praise name is Omu.

10 And she holds no Ndose. The Iyi is never the head of a temple and never the priest of a parish, and no Ndose is hers. Her authority does not come from a temple. It comes from the women's order, from Unako and Edem, and from Alo — the seat that runs the religion when the head dies.

11 And she is elected by the college of Eze Ana — the same body that elects and confirms the Ikala. The two heads are raised by one college, and the difference between them is not how they are raised but what they hold.

12 Eze Ana — the head of an Isiala, a diocese. He is the supreme authority in his territory and the chief interpreter of the divine will through afa.

13 Isiafa — the deacon, the head of an Okwu-Ana. He licenses the priests of his district and answers to the Eze Ana.

14 Ika Dibia — the chief priest of a Ndose. He leads all the ritual of the parish, heads every priest in it, and he runs and controls the Ndose.

15 And beneath him, four orders: Dibia Ana, the custodian of the earth · Dibia Afa, the diviner · Dibia Agwu, the calling · Dibia Ogwu, the healer.

16 And who may hold them. A woman may hold every one of those four orders, and each is conferred on her exactly as on a man. One office is reserved: the Ika Dibia. In rare cases a woman may hold it — where she has attained a high level of spirituality — and it is the diocesan council that confers it, not the Eze Ana alone and not the parish. And the Iyi may hold it as of right.

17 For the religion divides the two houses and gives each its own head. The Ndose is led by men, and Edem and Unako are led by women. A man does not head the healing house or the school, any more than a woman heads the temple. And neither house is a demotion — a Ndose without its Edem and its Unako is not a Ndose.

Chapter 2 — The calling

1 A priest is sought and not self-appointed. The priesthood is not hereditary. 2 The candidate must be of good standing, of clean habit, and of a quiet tongue. 3 He must be able to read the signs, and he must be able to keep silence about them. 4 And he is trained for twelve years in the Uko-Ndose, the seminary of the religion — longer than any other service in it, and the reason is that the work is not learned in a season. 5 And what he learns in those twelve years is four things: 6 The sixteen signs of afa, and their two hundred and fifty-six permutations — Book VI. 7 The properties of the leaves and the roots — for the healer's work and for the cleansing. 8 The code of cleanliness, which he keeps himself: he washes three times in the day, and his body, his cloth and his shrine are kept immaculate — for a priest whose own ground is foul has no standing to cleanse another's. 9 And the art of quiet presence. A Dibia does not run, and does not shout, and does not move chaotically; he moves deliberately and silently, as the python of Idemili moves. 10 And the seminary is not a place of honour. It is twelve years of the same discipline the religion asks of everybody, kept without a lapse — which is why the priest is licensed at the end of it, and not at the beginning.

Chapter 3 — The vestments and the emblems

1 White cloth, for the purity of his office. 2 The ofo, which is his authority, and which is given to him when his training is complete. 3 The eagle's feather, placed in his hair at his consecration, the sign that he speaks with the height of the truth and not with the weight of the ground. 4 And nothing that has touched blood, for his office is bloodless from the first day to the last.

Chapter 4 — The ordination

1 The candidate's standing is established. The cord-rite is performed for him, or his record of it is read — for that rite is the tradition's own bloodless rite of standing, and it demands no animal. 2 The ofo is conferred by the head of his diocese, or by the deacon of his district under the head's authority. Until that moment he may not officiate at anything. 3 And the consecration: the eagle feather, ugo, is placed in his hair, and the words are said over him:

"Ị bụzi oche Agwu. Eziokwu ka ị na-ekwu, n'agbanyeghị na ọ ga-ata gị ụta. Ọbara adịghị n'aka gị; ụgha

adịghị n'ire gị."

4 The priest rises, takes the ofo, and is given a new and secret name, known only to him and to his own chi. 5. And he is licensed in writing in the register of his Ndose, and his name is read aloud in the assembly, so that the community knows the man who will keep its rites and its confessions.

Chapter 5 — The taking of titles — Nze and Ozo

1 Ozo is not inherited. It is achieved and paid for, and it is open to any man who meets the requirements. It is not a caste and it is not a birthright. 2 The rungs below Ozo are three, and a man climbs them in order. 3 Ima Mmau, at about the age of nine. Three stages: the payment is made; the mask is revealed to him in the house of the masquerade — his hands, his feet, and last his face and his head; and then he is admonished. And the admonition is this: that to reveal what he has been shown is itikpo isi mmau — the breaking of the mask's skull — and it is a great abomination. 4 Ichi, or Ozo Ichi. Six stages: the payment; the exorcism; the marking of the face, where the cuts are made and the young man must try not to cry; twelve days of seclusion, during which the house is purified; the integration, in which an egg is broken to release him; and the appearance at the market with uli on the body. Then he is admonished again, and given the spear otonsi. 5 Nli Nwammadu, the novitiate. Three stages, and it is gated on marriage: a new name is taken; the first three paraphernalia are given; and he is told formally that Ozo lies ahead. 6 And then Ozo itself, in nine stages: Ofo Ozo → Obu nisi → Okpete → Ula Mmuo → Ikpata Ofo → Ido Mmuo / Ichi Ozo / Isa lie → Izu Afia → twenty-one days of seclusion → and the Ebo confession, and entry in the register. 7 The regalia are the outward form: the ankle cords, the ivory bangle, the eagle feather, the cowry, the staff. They are worn, and they are read — and the tradition holds that an Ozo man's kit is continuous with the ninth-century bronze and ivory of the old towns. 8 And the father-bar. In the old law a man might not take Ozo while his father lived. That bar was lifted long ago, and Odiana does not keep it. A son may take the title in his father's lifetime. 9 And the fees are set by the Ikala in council, for the old prices are recorded in the currency of another year and cannot be transferred as they stand.

Chapter 6 — Onu Ebo — the annual public confession

1 Once in the year, announced by the council, every titled person declares his wrongs in public, before the community. 2 This is not Nchegharị. The secret confession is between a person and the keeper, and it is never spoken of again. Onu Ebo is the opposite: it is said aloud, with the community standing. 3 How it is done. On the announced day the titled body assembles in the open, and the senior person present breaks the kola in the form of the rite. Then, in order of the rungs — the lowest first and the highest last — each one stands and says what he has done in the year that was wrong. 4 He names it, and he does not explain it away. He says what he did, and whom it touched, and what he proposes to do about it. 5 And the community may answer, and may ask, and may require restitution — for the declaration is not a performance of humility; it is the beginning of repair. 6 No one is struck, and no one is expelled for what he confesses. The person who confesses is doing what the order requires of him, and the order honours him for it. 7 And the one who conceals is the one in danger — for the tradition holds that concealment brings sickness first and then a death without honour, and the community holds it too, and watches. 8 And at the end, restitution is recorded, and the register of the year is closed, and the year begins again with the books of the titled body clean.

Chapter 7 — How the offices are filled

1 The Ikala is hereditary, from the royal lineage, and he is confirmed in public by the titled body and the college of the Eze Ana. The confirmation is open, and the people see the man. 2 The Iyi is taken from her own line, and her line keeps the rite of her taking. 3 An Eze Ana is raised to the diocese from among the licensed priests of that diocese, and his legitimacy is confirmed by the Ikala. 4 An Isiafa is appointed by the Eze Ana of the diocese, and takes his ofo from the Eze Ana's hand. 5 An Ika Dibia is appointed by the Isiafa of his district, and his name is licensed from the centre. 6 The four orders beneath him — Dibia Ana, Dibia Afa, Dibia Agwu, Dibia Ogwu — are appointed by the Ika Dibia from among those who have completed the training, and licensed by the Isiafa. 7 And no office is inherited except the headship of the religion itself. Custody is not priesthood: a Ndose's ground, fabric and goods are held by a custodian who is not its priest — for the tradition gives the temple to the firstborn to hold, and the office to the man who is fit for it. 8 And a licence is not a certificate. It is a conferral of ofo — authority from the ancestors — over a power that was never the licensee's own. And it can be withdrawn.

Chapter 8 — The Gift of Fire

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 The Harmattan lasted longer than anyone living could remember.

2 The cold dry wind came down, and came down again, and did not stop. The old and the young died in large numbers, and sorrow and grief covered the land. In the markets, and at the wakes for the dead, the people were cold and dull; and some of the men tried to keep warm by dancing the dance for the dead.

3 And the elders of the village met, and talked for a long time, and found nothing.

4 Then the oldest of them stood up and spoke.

"My people, I salute you. For many months you have withstood this suffering. Only Chukwu knows why we must go through it. Sometimes I wonder whether he has turned his face away from us.

Chukwu ought to be told of our plight. We must send a messenger to him."

5 The assembly accepted it. The hard question was who to send.

6 Mbe the tortoise offered to go. He had no wings, so the birds of the land fitted him with feathers — each bird giving one of its own — and he flew to Chukwu's land. It was a long and difficult flight, and he made it safely.

7 And at Chukwu's great gate he knocked, and waited.

8 There was no answer.

9 Mbe grew impatient, and began to drum on the door with his hands. And then he heard a loud voice from within, and it was a curse:

"Let those hands that knock stick to the door."

10 And Mbe answered it in anger:

"Let those words stick in your mouth."

11 And the gate stayed closed. He could not see Chukwu, and he came home empty-handed.

12 Then Nkita, the dog, offered to go.

13 At the great gate he did not drum, and he did not curse. He waited. And he was given a fire brand, and told to take it swiftly to the suffering people.

14 It turned out to be the hardest task anyone had undertaken. Nkita went back to Chukwu seven times with brands burned out — for he put the fire out with his own wet nose. And at the last, Chukwu taught him how to blow the fire gently, and so he carried it to his people.

15 And there was warmth and happiness all over the land.

16 But Nkita never got his breath back. He has been breathing fast ever since.

BOOK XI — The Book of Festivals (Emume Odiana)

(Annual cycle, holy days, cosmic seasons)

The year, the holy days, and how each is kept.

Chapter 1 — The week and the year

1 The week has four days: Eke, Oye, Afo, Nkwo. The days are persons and not numbers. 2 The year holds thirteen moons. 3 The council announces the year in Igu Aro, and no Ndose sets its own calendar. 4 The festival dates are computed from the moons, and the council publishes them.

Chapter 2 — Igu Aro — the announcing of the year

1 Igu Aro is the announcing of the year, and it is the second greatest season of the religion. It is kept at the head town, before the planting, and the whole land comes up to it.

2 And the year is not announced without blood. Igu Aro is a festival of the whole land, and every festival of this religion is kept with an animal killed. The year is a living thing being begun, and it is begun with a life given — as the land has always been approached, and as the year has always been opened.

3 The ground is renewed first: the surfaces are smoothed, the nzu is reapplied, the cloths are replaced, and everything worn is taken away and does not return.

4 And every household cleans its own compound and its own shrine, so that the year begins on clean ground.

5 Then the towns bring the tribute — and it is the towns that bring it, and not the council that buys it. Each Ndose brings what the custom requires.

6 And the customary portion is fixed, and the religion keeps it: one goat, one sheep, one fowl, sixteen yams, and eight kola. That is the bundle a town owes, and it has been the measure since it was set.

7 And a town that is great brings more — kine, and goats, and sheep, and fowl, and cowries, and yams — for a town brings what it has, and no town is shamed for bringing the measure and no more.

8 And the animal is killed in the open, at the place the council names, and its blood is spilled upon open ground and kept away from the shrine — for no blood is brought to the shrine in this religion. And the meat is cooked and shared that day, and no house that brought nothing is turned away from the eating. The tribute is not a tax, and the year is not begun by shaming anybody.

9 And the manner of the killing is part of the offering. It is done quickly, and without cruelty, and by a hand that knows how — for an animal tormented before its death has been taken badly, and the taking is half of the giving.

10 And the Dibia says over the killing what is said over every killing in this religion: that the animal is given and not merely taken; that it dies once; and that its life goes into the ground that feeds the town. The fowl carries the trouble away, and the beast feeds the people, and both are given.

11 And then the yam medicine is given out — ogwu ji — and the blessing of the year with it, and the towns carry both home to their own ground. No town plants before it has received them, for the head town holds the medicine of the yam.

12 And the head speaks the year aloud, and the towns answer.

13 And so the year is spoken, and fed, and the planting may begin.

14 And the religion keeps one thing plain about this day, since people will ask it. The animal is not a bribe and not a price. The year does not open because a beast was killed; the beast is killed because a year is being opened, and a beginning of this size is met with a life and not with words alone. And the religion does not teach that Chukwu is fed. Chukwu needs nothing. The ground is fed, and the ancestors are fed, and the people are fed, and that is the whole of it.

Chapter 3 — Ubi — the season of the farm

1 Ubi is the farm. And the Ubi is the season of it — the harvest festival of the religion, and the new yam, and more than the new yam. It is the greatest season of the year, and it is kept as a season and not as a day.

2 And it has three parts, as a year has its dry and its wet: the keeping before it, the feast itself, and the days after it. And no house eats of the new harvest until all three have begun.

3 And the season is fixed by the council, which publishes it at Igu Aro. No Ndose sets its own day for it.

The keeping before the Ubi — Ọnwa Ụbi

4 The month before the Ubi is kept as a fast of the ground. And the fast is not of meat but of new things.

5 In that month:

6 no new yam is dug except by the Ikala's word, and no new crop is eaten; 7 the ground of the compound, the market and the paths is cleaned to the edges, and the drains opened, and the walls mended; 8 the household puts its debts in order — what is owed is paid or spoken of with the person owed it — for the season is not entered carrying a debt; 9 what is not used is given away to a household that needs it, and this is Isalaka, of which more below; 10 the quarrels of the compound are settled low, before the feast and not at it; 11 and every person brings the tools of his work into repair, for the season is a season of the farm and not of idleness.

12 And a household that cannot keep the fast because of sickness, or age, or want, keeps what it can and says so plainly, and the Ndose does not shame it. The fast is kept by the strong for the sake of the whole, and the weak are carried by it.

13 And the meaning of the keeping is this: the season is not entered with a dirty ground, an unpaid debt, an unsettled quarrel, or a barn of things nobody will use. A person who arrives at the feast like that has not fasted; he has only waited.

The feast — Ụbọchị Ụbi

14 On the day the council names, the whole land keeps the Ubi.

15 What is brought.

16 Every household brings the first of what its own ground has given — not what was bought, and not what was given, but the first fruits of its own ubi. 17 Yam and cocoyam come first, for they are the chief crops of the land. 18 And then cassava, and maize, and the vegetables, and the fruit — one of each thing the household grows, however small. 19 A household that grew nothing brings water, and its portion is given to it with the rest. The festival is not a tax, and no house is shamed for a poor farm.

20 The offering — Isalaka.

21 Isalaka is the offering of this religion, and it is two things in one hand.

22 It is the gift, and it is the giving away. In the tradition it is the washing of a person's own hands by what he gives to another — and the religion keeps that whole, and keeps it first: to feed a person who cannot pay you back, to give and not be seen giving, to teach what you know to somebody who cannot buy it, and to make the giving a habit and not an event. And the gift is released — the person who received it must never become the giver's debtor. Do not say afterwards, "after everything I did for you." If repayment was the agreement, call it what it was.

23 And Isalaka is also the offering brought to the shrine — the first fruits, laid down whole. The first of the yam is not cut before it is offered.

24 The Dibia receives it at the Ndose, presents it on the altar with kola and with nzu, and pours the libation on the ground. And the Iyi receives the portion of the women's ground, and the two are offered together.

25 And the portions. A portion is set aside for the ancestors, and left at the ancestral place and not eaten by the household. A portion is set aside for the poor of the parish, and given on the day and not kept. And the household eats of what remains — so that the first thing it eats of the new harvest is the thing it has given away.

26 And the animal of the Ubi.

27 Once in the year, at the Ubi, and at no other time in the ordinary life of the religion, one animal may be killed for the feast — and it is killed as the ram is killed at the festival of the nations: in the open, by the household that brought it, and eaten by that household and its guests on the day.

28 And the animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground away from the shrine — and it is not brought to the altar at all, and nothing holy is touched with it. The altar keeps the kola, the nzu, the wine and the water — and the ground takes the blood, as it does at every killing of this religion.

29 And every household of the Ubi brings an animal if it has one — a fowl where that is what the house has, a goat where it can, and a beast where the house is great. And a household that cannot bring one brings what it has and keeps the Ubi fully, for the feast is the first fruits and the whole town eats.

30 And this is not the only killing in the year. Every festival of this religion is kept with an animal killed, and so is every serious rite — the announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The year is a round of givings, and a festival without an animal is a year that was not fed.

31 And the small rites of a house remain light — a birth, a naming, a marriage, a sickness, a private cleansing — and these are kept with kola, and nzu, and wine, and water, and with a fowl where the custom of the place asks for one. The religion does not kill at every turn. It gives a life where something is being begun, or bound, or put right.

32 And the strength. After the offering the young contend — wrestling, and the lifting of the heavy load, and the running of the four-day week's distance. The winner is honoured and the loser is not shamed. And the household that fed the most people that day is named aloud.

33 And the unity. The whole land eats together, and it eats in the open. No household eats behind a shut door, and no one is turned from the pot for want of a farm or a name.

The days after — Mgbe Ụbi

34 The Ubi is not over when the eating stops.

35 In the days after it:

36 the ground is swept and the sweepings carried away — the market, the paths, the Ndose and the courtyard; nothing is left overnight; 37 the husks and the bones are burned or buried, and nothing used is left at the edge of the ground; 38 the seed for the next planting is set apart before anything else is spent; 39 what the household owes to the shrine and to the poor is settled on the day it fell due; 40 and the poor of the parish are counted again, for the season has shown who they are.

41 And the doctrine of the Ubi, in one paragraph. The ground gave, and the household brings the first of it back before it tastes it. So the season is not a feast that happens to begin with a prayer. It is the recognition of a debt, and the feast is what follows. The land prepares; the land brings the first fruits; the land eats as one; and the land is left clean. And the one animal of the year is a household's own table and not an altar, and no man is made a debtor by a gift.

Chapter 4 — The water rite

1 At the season of the water, the people go to the river with white cloth, with clay vessels, and with aromatic leaves. 2 They wear white. They do not kneel and they do not bow. 3 The vessels are filled, the leaves are laid, and the priest speaks the blessing of Idemili. 4 And nothing that is used pollutes the land or the water. Whatever is carried to the river is carried home again.

Chapter 5 — The day of the ancestors

1 At the new moon, the family gathers at the ancestral place. 2 The elder cracks kola, calls the four names, and speaks the invocation. Nothing is killed. 3 The family eats together, and the names of the dead are spoken aloud, so that they are not forgotten.

Chapter 6 — The offering to the chi

1 The offering to men's chi and the offering to women's chi are separate rites, and each is led by its own order. 2 The men's is led by the priest, and the women's by the Iyi or by the woman she appoints. 3 Each person brings kola and water, and gives thanks for the year.

Chapter 7 — The Wrestler Whose Back Never Touched the Ground

A story of Igu Aro, and the contest.

1 It was the last day of Igu Aro — the festival that marks the beginning of the planting season and foretells the fate of the year to come.

2 And on the day before, the diviner had announced that the year ahead would be fruitful, so the people were ready to celebrate the good news.

3 And on that last day the wrestling was held.

4 And this is how it was done. The crowded market was cleared out. A circle was dug in the ground and filled with soft sand, and that was where the wrestling would take place. The people sat and stood around the circle, and a flute player sat on a stool at the front of the crowd. He brought the flute to his lips and began to play, and two boys walked to the middle of the circle.

5 And there was a wrestler whose back had never touched the ground.

6 No one had thrown him. No one had pinned him. Not once, in all the years — and the town had come to expect it, and the young men had come to fear it, and the older men had begun to say quietly that it was not skill but luck, and that luck runs out.

7 And on that day he was thrown.

8 And the crowd was silent, and the flute stopped, and the man lay on his back in the soft sand of the circle.

9 And then he stood up, and he laughed, and he took the hand of the man who had thrown him and held it up before the whole town, and he said:

"Today the year is fruitful. And today I am a man who was thrown, and I am still standing. Let the year

be judged by the standing and not by the falling."

10 And the town shouted, and the flute began again, and the planting began.

Chapter 8 — The War of the Sky and the Earth

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 Years came and went, and the war between the sky and the earth raged on.

2 The weak took refuge in the evil groves, or were taken, and sold.

3 A warrior-father was leaving his house, and he turned at the door and warned his children:

"Children, be warned. Enemy soldiers roam our land. Do not, my little dears, let smoke off, or indeed raise your voices. Everything you need is in the house. I shall be back shortly."

4 The children had lost their mother in a raid the year before.

5 And as soon as their father was gone from the house, they turned deaf ears to everything he had told them.

6 And the two fighting groups came down on them. The forces of the sky seized the boy, Omaludo. The warriors of the earth took the girl, Odede.

7 Omaludo lived and grew in the house of a stern slave dealer. He suffered hardship there, from his master and from his fellow slaves. And young as he was, he decided to run away. Night after night he walked, further and further from his master and from his people. And the hardship turned the boy into a brave man.

8 He came at last to safety and freedom in a far country, where the tale of the war and the sorrow of the slave trade were strange things to hear. There he found a master, an itinerant craftsman, who said to him:

"If you live well with my wife and children, I will do all in my power for you."

9 Within a few days of his coming, the mistress of that house went to a distant market at dusk, and left him the housekeeping. And when she came back in the evening the children hardly noticed her — they were too happy with their new boy. And there was food ready, and she ate it. And she said to herself:

"Let me hope that this is good luck. This kind of luck does not exist today."

10 In the night she went to her friend and neighbour, and the two of them talked about the new houseboy. The friend had noticed something, and would not say what it was. She said only:

"You should see for yourself. The world is very deep indeed."

11 The young woman lay thinking about it, and the morning was very slow in coming. At first cockcrow she was up, and she took her basket and went out.

12 And at dawn Omaludo swept the house and the compound clean with dried palm leaves, and worked in the kitchen before the children woke. He washed them and he fed them. The youngest cried, and the boy held it and sang for it. And he used the pestle and the mortar as he sang, for the sound of it, because the sound was the sound of his father's house:

"Kwa kpom, kwa kpom — de gululu de.

Lost brother and sister … do not cry, child.

Long, long ago, Father gave us yam.

He warned us against the puffs of dark smoke.

He warned us against the pounding — kwa kpom —

for over our thatch hung thick dark smoke.

Odede pounded … kwa kpom.

The war of the sky appeared.

The war of the earth appeared.

The sky seized Omaludo.

The earth took Odede.

Lost brother and sister … do not cry, child."

13 And Odede was wild with joy — for Omaludo was her lost brother. She had followed everything the boy did, from her friend's house, since dawn. She leapt over the low wall that separated her from her brother, and fell on him.

14 And the two of them looked at each other in silence, and in amazement.

15 And the story of Odede and Omaludo spread through that whole neighbourhood. And the people said:

"Truly, blood does not tell a lie."

BOOK XII — The Book of Wisdom (Okwu Amamihe)

(Sayings, proverbs, parables, teachings)

Sayings, proverbs, parables and teachings.

Chapter 1 — The sayings

1 The person who sweeps his own ground has no need to be told that his neighbour's is dirty. 2 A kola nut shared is a debt recorded; a kola nut kept is a debt forgotten. 3 The mouth that eats alone will one day speak alone. 4 Water does not argue with the pot; it either boils or it does not. 5 The child who asks questions is not rude. The elder who cannot answer is not shamed. 6 What the eye has seen, the mouth should not deny. 7 A path is made by walking it, and a name is made by answering to it. 8 The goat that eats the yam is not the goat that pays for it — meaning that a community answers for the wrong of one of its own. 9 When the moon is full the dog barks at it; the moon does not stop.

Chapter 2 — The parables

1 The two brooms. A man swept his courtyard with one palm rib and it took him till noon. His neighbour bound forty ribs together and swept hers before the sun was up. Neither rib was stronger than the other. The binding was the strength. So it is with a lineage, and so it is with a town. 2 The pot that was filled. A woman drew water every morning and filled her pot to the brim. It cracked in the third month, and she blamed the pot. Her neighbour filled hers to the shoulder and carried it three years. What a person does every day without rest is not devotion. It is a crack, and it will open. 3 The kola that was counted. A man broke kola for eleven people. He counted the pieces aloud and found twelve, and said so. And the twelfth piece was his own, which he had forgotten. So a person who counts what he has given away has counted himself out of the giving. 4 The dog and the shrine. A dog slept at the door of the Ndose every night and never entered. The priest said to him, You are the holiest animal in this town. And the dog said, I am also the dirtiest, and that is why I sleep outside. A clean ground is not kept by those who cannot enter it. It is kept by those who keep it. 5 The boundary that moved. A man moved his neighbour's stone by one pace, in the night, and slept well. The next year he moved it by one more, and slept well. In the ninth year he stood up and found that he had no neighbour, and that the land he had taken went to the edge of the bush, and that nothing grew on it. What a person takes by a pace at a time is taken from himself, and the ground remembers the pace. 6 The child who would not be washed. A child was brought to the water at the threshold and refused it, and was brought again, and refused again. And his mother did not force him. She washed herself, and entered, and left the door open. And in the evening he washed and came in. The religion does not drag anybody across its threshold. It keeps the water there and leaves the door open. 7. The two drums. One drum was kept in a dry room and oiled, and beaten at the festival. The other was kept by a man who beat it whenever he was angry. At the festival the first drum spoke, and the second only rattled. The mouth that is used for rage will not be believed when the matter is serious.

Chapter 3 — The wisdom liturgy

Said at the opening of a school of the Ndose, and before an elder gives counsel.

1 We do not begin with our own wisdom. We begin with the ground, and with the ones who walked it before us. What we know, we were taught. What we were taught, we must keep. Let the elder speak and the young one hear. Let the young one ask and the elder not be shamed. For the path is made by walking it, and the covenant is kept by keeping it. The kola is broken, and the ground receives the wine.

Chapter 4 — The Tortoise and the Birds

A folktale of the Igbo, read in the law.

1 There was a famine, and the animals grew thin. The antelope and the deer grew lean on the browning grass, and the leopard grew thin from the lack of prey. Some built nests and dug caves, and some stored fat, and the python went deep into sleep to wake only when the earth was bountiful again.

2 And everyone suffered except Mbeku, the tortoise.

3 For the tortoise noticed that the birds stayed the same. Their feathers were still fluffed, and while the other animals began to show their bones through their skins, the birds grew healthier and more robust.

4 And the tortoise had run out of the food he had stored, so he went to the cuckoo bird — who was known for being proud — and he knew exactly how to talk to him.

5 And he said: "I have noticed that your feathers still shine as they did before the famine!"

6 And the bird came down.

7 And the tortoise talked his way into the feast of the birds, and got them to lend him feathers so that he could fly with them. And he told them to give him a name, and he gave himself the name "All of you" — so that when the birds in the sky were told "this feast is for all of you", the tortoise would eat it all.

8 And the tortoise ate the best of everything, and the birds went hungry.

9 And when the birds saw the trick, they took back their feathers — each one taking the feather he had lent — and the tortoise was left in the sky with nothing to fly on.

10 And he fell.

11 And the parrot was sent ahead to tell the tortoise's wife to spread soft things under the house for her husband to land on — and the parrot told her the opposite, and she brought out the hard things: the pestles, the mortars, the hoes and the stones.

12 And the tortoise fell on them and broke his shell, and that is why the tortoise's shell is in pieces to this day.

Chapter 5 — Why the Alligator Lives Alone

A folktale of the Igbo, with its song. Read in the law.

1 There was a famine in the animal kingdom, and seven of them met in the middle of a forest with a plan.

2 The vulture began it, and with him were the crocodile, and the pig, and the antelope, and the dog, and the chicken, and the rabbit. And every one of them had skin stretched too thin across its body, and the vulture and the chicken had bare patches where their feathers should have been.

3 And the alligator was the only one of them that could hunt in the rivers — and because of that he had managed to keep from starving, though he knew that he would run out of food soon.

4 And the seven made their agreement, and set their day, and went their ways.

5 And the alligator did not keep it.

6 Now the animals had a song for him, and the children of the town sang it:

Ngweleaghuli o lacha nbembe kai na! — Olacha!

Ndi gu na fa yi alacha nbembe a na ba si go! — Olacha!

"Alligator, eater of berries, let us go. The people who came with you to eat the berries have left."

7 And the alligator lives alone to this day. He keeps to the water and to his own stretch of bank, and the animals do not call on him, and he does not call on them.

Chapter 6 — The Pit at Eke Nza

A folktale of the Igbo.

1 There was a girl whose beauty was spoken of in every compound of the town, and her name was Nwa Ineene.

2 And she knew it. She was beautiful, and she was proud with it — and pride is ikpa nganga, and the Igbo do not carry it well.

3 And the young women of the town took counsel against her, because her beauty had made them small in their own eyes. They did not say that. That is how envy works — it finds a reason afterwards.

4 And they decided on a death. They chose the path that led to the dance at Eke Nza, and they dug a pit there, deep and wide, and covered it over — and they told her friend nothing, because her friend would have told her.

5 And on the day of the dance she went down that path with the others.

6 And the young men who were in the plot took her, and threw her into the pit, and ran on to the dance.

7 And Nwa Ineene lay at the bottom of the pit and sang.

"E, Nwa Ineene, E, Nwa Ineene dara olulu.

"E, Nwa Ineene, E, Nwa Ineene dara olulu.

"Ụkwụ kpọọ gị n'ụzọ, ị kpọrọ Ineene dara olulu."

Ineene's child has fallen into the pit. And she sang the road itself into the song — the foot that took her there.

8 And her mother began to look for her, and found nothing. And she went out on the road and called, and at a distance she heard the song, faint — and she went on, and the song grew clearer, and at the place where the pit was, the owl called out and she knew. And she cried, "Nwa Ineene m o!" — my child! — and the girl answered her out of the ground, and sang her song again with her mother's name in it.

9 And her friend came looking, and heard it too, and went down on her knees in the bush and searched until she found the mouth of the pit. And then her father came, and heard it, and found them.

10 And they could not lift her out. She had no strength left in her, and the pit was deep.

11 And they sent for the strongest rope in the town, and tied it to a great tree, and her friend climbed down into the pit and tied the rope about her, and they drew her up.

12 And when she came home they gave her medicine, and she was not well for a long time. And the beauty was still hers, but the pride was gone.

13 From that day she did not carry herself above anybody, and she greeted whoever she met on the road — and that is the whole of what the tale was told for.

BOOK XIII — Mkpụrụ Odinana

(The Motto of Odinana Igbo)

Chapter 1 — The Three Pillars (Ogidi Atọ)

1 From wisdom comes foundation; from foundation comes right living. 2 Odinana rests upon three pillars, given from the beginning and confirmed by the ancestors. These are Nsọ Ana, Ntọ Ana,, and Iwu Ana. Whoever holds these holds the covenant; whoever neglects them walks outside the shelter of Ana. 3 Nsọ Ana — the Sacredness of Earth. Ana is not soil to be consumed but a womb to be honored. Her hills are bones, her rivers are veins, her silence is memory. To wound Ana is to wound the mother of all life. Nsọ Ana teaches that every step is a prayer, every harvest a reckoning, and every grave a returning. 4 Ntọ Ana — the Foundation upon Earth. Before a house stands, its foundation is laid. Before a people endure, their feet must know the ground. Ntọ Ana is the ancestral wisdom tested by time: the customs that hold community, the rites that anchor the living to the living Earth, the truths that do not shift with seasons. Without foundation, even the tallest tree falls. 5 Iwu Ana — the Law that Flows from Earth. Law is not a burden but a path. Iwu Ana is the wisdom of aeons made visible: the taboo that protects blood, the oath that guards speech, the boundary that preserves peace, the care that shelters the weak. To walk Iwu Ani is to walk with balance, knowing that every choice carries weight and every action leaves a mark upon Ana. 6 Thus stands the word of Odinana, unchanged by time, upheld by those who remember.

Chapter 2 — The Charge (Nduzi)

1 Observe them. Let no hand defile what Chukwu called forth. Let no generation abandon the wisdom of those who came before. Let no heart choose ease over righteousness. 2 Stay intune with Nature. For Nature is not separate from the sacred. The rains that fall, the soil that bears, the seasons that turn, these are not forces to be conquered but voices to be heard. When humanity forgets Nature, it forgets itself. When humanity honors Nature, it honors Chukwu, who set the rhythms and named the balance. 3 Let this be the motto held by every child of Ana, every keeper of the covenant: Nsọ Ani, Ntọ Ani, Iwu Ani — Observe them. Stay intune with Nature. Walk in the Light of Chukwu with clean hands and a true heart. 4 Let no heart tremble at the closing of the eyes. For just as the sun sets only to rise, the soul departs only to return. The wicked fear death because they know their next shell will be hard. The righteous welcome death because they know their next shell will be honorable. 5 Teach your children: 'When you see the spear, do not see death; see the doorway. When you hear the thunder of war, do not hear your end; hear the drums of Ana mmụọ calling you to council.' 6 To die protecting the land is to secure a swift rebirth. The coward rots in a slow cycle; the brave returns in a single generation. Stand firm, therefore, knowing that Chukwu does not break His vessels—He reshapes them. -

THE THIRD PART — THE RITE AND THE CONFESSION

BOOK XVI — The Breaking of Kola (Iwa Oji)

Chapter 1 — Iwa Oji, the Breaking of the Kola

The rite that opens every gathering of Odiana. This is how it is done.

1 Nothing in the religion begins without it. No meeting, no council, no rite, no festival and no session of afa — the kola is broken first.

2 Who breaks it. In any gathering of men and women together, the kola is broken by the oldest man present — no matter what. Not by the highest in rank, and not by a titled woman, and not by the Iyi, and not by the Ikala himself if an older man is in the room. The kola is not rank. It is age, and it is the oldest man there.

3 And in a gathering of women only, the kola is broken by the oldest woman present, and the words and the order are exactly the same.

4 Both a man and a woman may break kola and pray over it, and the prayer is the same prayer. The only difference between them is the room. A woman breaks kola among women, and never in a general gathering; and in a general gathering the oldest man breaks it, whatever his standing and whatever hers.

5 And the rule does not change with the place. The Eze Ana breaks the kola of his diocese and the Ika Dibia the kola of his parish because each is the oldest man in the room he convenes — and where he is not, the oldest man present breaks it, and the senior in rank is served first.

6 What is needed. A kola nut · a small bowl of palm wine or of water · and a calabash or small vessel to pour from.

7 The order of the rite:

8 The kola is held up, so that all present can see it. 9 The senior person thanks Chukwu first, and names him by his own name and not by any other. 10 Then the earth is thanked — Ana for her bounty. 11 Then the sky — for the rain. 12 Then the thunder — Amadioha, for guidance and for discipline. 13 Then the harvest — Ìfèjiọkụ for what the ground has given. 14 And then the alusi who were not named directly are named together, so that none is left out and none is offended. 15 And while the names are said, the wine is poured on the ground. Not into a vessel, and not into a cup: on the ground. 16 Then the senior person thanks those gathered for coming, and says why they are met. 17 And the kola is broken and shared, and the order of the sharing is the order of the room — the senior first, then by age and by title, and no one who is present is left out.

18 And where those gathered are not one another's kin — which is most of the time in a Ndose — the senior person states the order aloud before he serves, for the tradition's own rule is that "an expanded model is invented to accommodate the new situation."

19 And a kola is never served to exclude. If there is one kola and ten people, it is divided into ten.

BOOK XVII — The Creed of Odiana (Nkwenye Odiana)

Chapter 1 — Nkwenye Odiana, the Creed

Said standing, facing east, at the beginning of the day and at the opening of an assembly.

1 I hold the ofo and I am clean.

2 I believe in Chukwu, who was not made and does not end, who is light without flame and thought without a tongue.

3 I believe in Ana, the mother earth, called also Ana, and Anị in the old speech — the great womb, and the bearer of consequence, and the ground whose memory is the law.

4 And I believe that Ana is the way, and that through her the heart of Chukwu is reached, and that there is no other road to it. She is the mother, and the door, and the first shrine of every person born of her.

5 And therefore, to become an Odianian, a person must believe in Ana. This is the one belief that is required of anyone, and it is the whole of the requirement — and everything else in this creed is what follows from it.

6 I believe that Anị makes the new souls and receives the old, and sends them back at the right time — and so I do not fear the closing of my eyes.

7 I believe in the ancestors, the Unseen Seen, the roots of the living tree, who examine my hands and not my words.

8 I believe that my chi speaks and does not shout, and that my hand must answer it.

9 I believe that afa is the way the will of Chukwu is known among men, and that a reading which does not answer the question is not a reading.

10 I believe that ıwu is made and nso is given, and that a thing done by law is not the same as a thing inherited — and I will not be told otherwise.

11 I believe that the life of an animal is given at the festivals of this religion and at its serious rites, and that the blood goes to the ground and not over the altar, and that what is laid on the altar is kola, and white chalk, and the wine, and the water. And I believe that no human blood is ever shed in this religion, in violence or in rite, for it was the spilling of human blood on the earth that made the earth sacred in the first place.

12 I believe that the ground remembers, that the poor are not to be left, and that the wrong I do is owed to the whole community and not only to the one I wronged.

13 I believe in the clean ground, the clean hand, and the clean word, and I will keep them.

14 And I will keep the kola, and the nso, and the days of the week, and the name of my lineage.

15 Isee.
